speechtext:

I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis):
That the government abandon its plan to import non-Canadian workers for Canadian jobs and devise another, obviously more sensible plan which would give unemployed Canadians opportunities to fill these vacancies.

subsubtopic: RECRUITMENT OF SKILLED WORKERS FROM ABROAD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Employment and Immigration, in the absence of the Minister of State for External Relations who takes his place, and in the absence of the Minister of Labour who takes his place, I will direct my question to the Right Hon. Prime Minister. Recently the Minister of Employment and Immigration made a statement telling us that 20,000 to 25,000 skilled workers will be hired abroad this year and will be brought into Canada because, according to him, there is a shortage of skilled labour in the Canadian labour market. Could the Prime Minister please inform the House how he arrived at those figures?
March 29, 1982

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: RECRUITMENT OF SKILLED WORKERS FROM ABROAD
speechtext: Madam Speaker, this is a question of a statistical nature, and I will have to take notice of it.

Madam Speaker, I would assume that when a minister makes a statement about importing 20,000 to 25,000 skilled labourers when there are over one million unemployed, the Prime Minister would take some interest in it.
Hear, hear!

Perhaps the parliamentary secretary would know more about it than the Prime Minister. Would he perhaps answer the question and tell us from where he got those figures, and on what they were based? Where are Canadians, such as Len Prevost who just graduated from a skilled course in computer programming and cannot find employment, to find the jobs about which the minister is talking?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I pointed out that it was the statistical character of the answer which caused me difficulty, not the substance of it. As the minister has explained before-and I have talked about it-the educational system in Canada is not geared to jobs of the future. I believe the minister gave a few examples which I have in mind. One was that Ontario Hydro is looking for-and I forget the number of engineers-a great number of engineers. They have to be brought in from abroad because our schools in Canada, our universities, have not produced sufficient numbers of engineers. Another example I remember him giving was in the case of the province of Alberta where literally hundreds of engineers are needed. Application is made to the Department of Immigration so that we can bring in these engineers from abroad, because our technical schools have not produced a sufficient number of them.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STIMULATION THROUGH LOWERING OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the Prime Minister a question. I think it is well known that in almost every single industrial sector unemployment is rising dramatically, whether it be the steel industry, the farm implement industry, the footwear industry, the auto industry, the appliance industry, or for that matter general construction, and housing in particular, and that there are fewer and fewer job opportunities for Canadians. In every single instance the main reason cited for the downturn is the high interest rate policy of the government.
March 29, 1982

In the interest of this country is there no measure that can be taken by this government to reduce the interest rates chargeable on those products that Canadians should be purchasing but are not purchasing because they cannot afford them? Is there no measure that can be taken by this government to enable those Canadians to get work who should be working and who are not working because there are no people to purchase what they would be making? Is there no way we can bring down interest rates in Canada and thereby stimulate our economy and provide Canadians with some hope?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STIMULATION THROUGH LOWERING OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Yes, Madam Speaker, there is a way. The Minister of Finance has referred to it many times. I have referred to it many times. The way would be to bring down inflation, to bring down costs, and when the cost of money is lower, the cost of borrowing money will be lower.

subtopic: RATIONALE FOR REDUCING COST OF BORROWING MONEY
RATIONALE FOR REDUCING COST OF BORROWING MONEY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, is the Prime Minister aware that the cost of money is one of the main contributing factors to the end cost of the product and that carrying charges, both for industry and for the retailer, are a major contributing factor to the final price in the retail store? Surely by reducing interest rates we will reduce the price of a product and thereby increase the purchasing power of Canadians. Does that rationale not make sense?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: RATIONALE FOR REDUCING COST OF BORROWING MONEY
speechtext: Yes it does, Madam Speaker. That is why we are attempting to put downward pressure on inflation, thereby reducing the cost of money, thereby reducing interest rates, and thereby giving stimulus to the economy. That makes sense, Madam Speaker. But the hon. member has to realize that to bring down inflation it takes more than asking questions about the rate of interest. We have to make sure that inflation is lower and that inflationary expectations are lower. In that case we will have lower interest rates.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT INTEREST RATES BE REDUCED BY LEGISLATIVE ACTION
REQUEST THAT INTEREST RATES BE REDUCED BY LEGISLATIVE ACTION
speechtext:

Surely it makes sense to try that measure, rather than to continue with what is now affecting so many hundreds of thousands of Canadians so detrimentally,

speechtext: In view of the fact that the scope of the War Measures Act violates not only the International Convenant on Civil and Political Rights, but also the new Charter of Rights, will the minister assure the House that any new legislation will, in fact, repeal the provisions of the War Measures Act? speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: INQUIRY ON TIMETABLE FOR INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member knows perfectly well that the order in council to which he is referring was made public last May and put before a federal-provincial conference of ministers responsible for emergency measures planning. The order in council was merely an update of another order in council dating back to 1965, which also contained provisions for civilian internment. In fact, the provisions were in effect in 1979, under the Progressive Conservative government, who did not see fit to modify them. As a result, we see no reason to change what we see as a bare minimum of provisions for the sound planning of emergency measures in this country. As for future legislation, officials of Privy Council are now looking into the matter. I also intend to carry out a thorough consultation of provincial authorities to avoid overstepping any jurisdictional boundaries, and when everything is ready, the hon. member will be notified, but it is not going to be ready next week!

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Prime Minister. When the Prime Minister invoked the War Measures Act in 1970, he trampled on and overrode the fundamental rights protected by the Canadian Bill of Rights.
It was Parliament.

He now proclaims that the Charter of Rights will protect Canadians from abuses under the emergency planning order which, among other things, will allow him to impose sweeping censorship and to commandeer all media for an unlimited period of time.
Is the Prime Minister prepared to assure the House that under no circumstances will his government make use of the "notwithstanding" clause in the Charter of Rights to deny, during times of emergency, the fundamental rights of all
Oral Questions
Canadians, or is the Charter of Rights to become as useless during times of emergency as was the Canadian Bill of Rights when the Prime Minister said, "Just watch me", in 1970?
Oh, oh!

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would first point out to the hon. member that the War Measures Act was adopted in 1970 with the concurrence of hon. members on both sides of this House.
With information withheld.

Second, the "notwithstanding" clause was brought into the Charter, as the hon. member knows, at the insistence of the provinces. The federal government had a Charter which did not have a "notwithstanding" clause. I am sorry that the hon. member, personally, if my recollection is correct, did not support it. I would hope that that hon. member would use his influence to get Premier Blakeney, along with other premiers, to revert to the original bill that we had.

speechtext: Did the government enter into negotiations with other nations and their major airlines regarding the utilization of the Winnipeg International Airport as either a stopover point or a major departure centre on the so-called "polar route" to Europe and, if so, at what location and on what date were the meetings held and were any agreements reached?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, March 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacEachen that Bill C-97, to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977, and to provide for payments to certain provinces, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in my remarks on Bill C-97, last Friday I discussed some of the highlights of the bill itself and also the role of the operation of the parliamentary task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements which sat last spring and summer studying
Federal Transfers to Provinces
this very important issue. In the next few minutes I would like to discuss some of the recommendations of the task force regarding health care and post-secondary education.
As previously mentioned, in his speech on this bill in the House on March 22, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) stated that negotiations with respect to clarification of national standards for health care and efficient mechanisms for their maintenance should be worked out with the provinces by March 31, 1983, and that ways of implementing national objectives with respect to post-secondary education should be worked out with the provinces by March of 1984.
With respect to the health care system the task force believes that the achievement of comprehensive, publicly-funded hospital, medical and extended health care is a major accomplishment of Canadian society which represents the end of a long struggle for the realization of an ideal. It concluded that there is an overriding national interest in the operation of health insurance plans and in the effectiveness of health care delivery and that the proper role for the federal government is the formulation, monitoring and enforcement of conditions on its financial support of provincial programs.
The task force also concluded that in aggregate and in present circumstances federal government funding for health care services in Canada appears to be generally adequate. It recommended that after consultation with the provincial governments the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) should undertake a consolidation of the existing legislation in order to establish clear program conditions supported by explicit criteria against which satisfaction of those program conditions can be monitored. Thus, in case federal-provincial negotiations fail to achieve agreement on program conditions, the task force would expect provisions for some withholding of federal financial support to provincial plans which do not meet fully those conditions as interpreted in the report.
The task force also concluded that retention of the present block funding arrangement, with stricter conditions, monitoring and enforcement mechanisms, would provide an effective mechanism to ensure compliance with national program conditions. We recommend for this purpose the establishment of operational program criteria, perhaps monitored by a parliamentary committee or a national health council, with federal payments on condition that there be compliance with program criteria-but conditional in a flexible manner, that is, with a graduated holdback of federal transfers related to the effect of program conditions.
In addition, we concluded that hospital and medical care premiums constitute a regressive form of taxation and that their use for financing a service as basic as health care is regrettable. We recommended that a clear definition and measurement of universality of coverage be developed to ensure that the principle of universality is respected. While recognizing the right of provincial governments to levy premiums, the task force agreed that prior payment of premiums

March 29, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
should not be a precondition of entitlement to treatment. We agreed that for reasons of both principle and practicality user fees for hospitals should be discouraged.
All the above recommendations, agreements and conclusions with respect to our health care system were the unanimous opinion of our seven-man task force. The remaining recommendations were the opinion of the majority of the task force and were not unanimous. The majority recommended that doctors who bill a provincial medical plan directly or whose patients are reimbursed by the plan not be allowed to charge fees in excess of those permitted under the plan's approved fee schedule. The majority concurred in the recommendations of Mr. Justice Emmett Hall that the Medical Care Act should be revised to provide that extra billing by physicians inhibits reasonable access to services and is contrary to the intents and purposes of the act and that the provinces should develop mechanisms to ensure reasonable compensation to physicians.
The majority also agreed with Mr. Justice Hall's proposal that if negotiations between a province and physicians fail, then the issues should be decided by binding arbitration with a board of three persons: an independent chairperson to be named by the chief justice of the province, one nominee from the medical profession and one from the provincial government. The majority also recommended that following federal-provincial negotiations any plan which does not meet fully all the above criteria should be ineligible for full federal financial support under EPF.
There are other important recommendations of the task force with respect to the health care system, including emphasis on the broad health field concept and the community-based health care philosophy, which are also set out in our report.
With respect to the transfer of Government of Canada funds for post-secondary education, the task force was unanimous in its recommendations. We recognized the need for general base funding for the post-secondary sector to permit adults of all ages-not just those in the traditional 18 to 24 age group-to pursue spiritual and intellectual goals, to polish their critical faculties and to expand their general base of knowledge on which more specific skills may be built. Appreciating that education is under provincial jurisdiction, the task force believed that there should be an effective consultation mechanism to ensure concerted effort by all concerned to establish and obtain goals that are of mutual interest to both orders of government. It recommended that, in line with the 1976 first ministers' commitment, the responsible federal minister or ministers proceed on an urgent basis to conduct with the council of ministers of education on matters of concern to both orders of government in the field of higher education.
The task force suggested that early attention be given to the definition of "purposes in post-secondary education" and that priority consideration be given to the need for more highly qualified manpower in the 1980s, and for the confirmation of existing commitments to student mobility and equality of access to post-secondary education for Canadians. We recommended that the current block-funded basis be continued, at
least for the time being, but that the post-secondary education program be separate from the future support of health programs.
We recommended that there should be federal-provincial discussions for improving assistance to needy students, described in the report of the task force on student assistance, and we agreed that there should be more public information made available on general federal government support to the provinces for post-secondary education.
The task force also unanimously recommended that the federal minister responsible report annually to Parliament with respect to federal transfers to each province for higher education, other federal support to post-secondary education, the effectiveness of these programs in moving toward the country's economic and other goals, the results of consultations with the council of provincial ministers of education about the definition of "national purposes to be served by higher education", and the means by which these objectives will be achieved. Additional recommendations can be found in our report with respect to post-secondary education.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to state that I strongly support Bill C-97 for the reasons mentioned in the first part of my comments last Friday afternoon. I am pleased that the more disadvantaged parts of our great country will continue to be dealt with very fairly by greatly increased equalization payments being made to them, and that the federal government's commitment to health care and post-secondary education also continues to be strongly shown. As mentioned before, these Government of Canada payments for equalization, health care and post-secondary education will amount to about $105 billion in cash and tax points to the provinces over the next five years and, as also mentioned, our task force wanted to make sure that there was full accountability to the people of Canada for this $105 billion that will be flowing directly to the provinces.
Our proposals and recommendations with respect to our health care and post-secondary education systems, some of which I have enumerated above, were developed to try to ensure this greater accountability. I therefore hope and trust that, during federal-provincial negotiations with respect to health care and post-secondary education over the next one and two years, our comments in our report and our recommendations with respect to these two most important fields will be carefully considered. I also hope and trust that the result will be stronger and more effective health care and post-secondary education systems that will be much more accountable than now to the people of Canada.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have looked forward to speaking very briefly on this important subject of federal-provincial fiscal transfers. Other speakers have said that it is this type of system which holds confederation together in Canada. I am sure there are many elements of truth in that statement. Without this type of system, each
March 29, 1982

province would be on its own. Fiscally, there would be very little to bring us all together as one country. It is only right that the more wealthy parts of the nation should in some way help to subsidize those parts that are not as well off and that find themselves in conditions below the average. It is an integral part of the Canadian system as we know it.
I have one comment to make about this, however. I do not think that fiscal transfers should have been entrenched in the Constitution. It makes sense to me to have them but surely we can achieve them under ordinary acts of Parliament. I do not think it was necessary to entrench in the Constitution of Canada the provisions for federal-provincial fiscal transfers. However, Mr. Speaker, that argument is over now, and when the new Constitution arrives we will find this provision entrenched in it.
In the long run it will probably work to our disadvantage as it will be maintained that the system we have today should remain forever. I hope that at some point we will find that it is not necessary to maintain this system. It has worked reasonably well for us, but because we have put it in the Constitution we will find it difficult to change. These administrative arrangements can best be dealt with by ordinary statute and legislation, in my opinion.
I should like to compliment the parliamentary Task Force on Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements which was put together at the request of Parliament. Certain changes were proposed by the federal government but it was Parliament that decided they should not be enacted until they had been carefully considered. Good work was done by members of all parties on that task force. In particular, I think of the work done by the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blen-karn) and the hon. member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker), which was exemplary. Of course, good work was also done by all members of the task force.
One of the good things that came out of the task force study, in an area in which I took a great deal of interest, was that the task force took the time to visit not only the provinces but also the two territories. The fiscal relationships of the territories with the federal government are just as important as those with the provinces. In fact, in a way they are more so, because the territories are in the process of development and change.
Some time ago the Hon. C. M. Drury devoted two years of study and attention to the fiscal relationships that exist between the Northwest Territories and the Government of Canada. He was the Prime Minister's special representative on constitutional development in the Northwest Territories and a lot of his study was devoted to the financial relationships that exist between the territorial and the federal governments. I should like to quote from Mr. Drury's report on this subject. He came to the following conclusion in paragraph 6.6, at page 124 of his report:
New arrangements should provide for the calculation of an annual general purpose grant at a non-discretionary level, as an alternative to the general federal subsidies for operating and capital costs. Except in extraordinary circumstances, the onus should be on the territorial government to raise any additional funds required through taxation or borrowing. These arrangements should also be
Federal Transfers to Provinces
effective for longer than the present one-year duration of federal-territorial financial agreements. To support any necessary borrowings or unexpected year-to-year volatility in territorial tax revenues, the revenue stabilization program should be extended to the NWT

I think that is an important observation. Most provinces can take part in the revenue stabilization program. From time to time when provincial revenues fluctuate widely, the program would allow the ministers of finance of all provinces to plan carefully knowing that there will not be wide variations in the amount of money that accrues to the Consolidated Revenue Fund in their particular province. It is a good program that is operated by the federal government. In my opinion and in the opinion of Mr. Drury, it should be extended to the territories and I hope that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) will see fit to do so at some time.
Mr. Drury also went on to say:
-and the governor in council should initially retain the power to approve proposed GNWT borrowings. However, this latter power should rarely be exercised as a veto. Its purpose would be to increase the credit rating of the GNWT as a preferred borrower.
I think that is a step in the right direction. Most provinces use their capacity to borrow on financial markets, both in Canada and abroad, for good provincial purposes. For instance, we can look at provincial hydro authorities, one of the largest borrowers. It would be a step toward normal provincial-type responsibility in the territories if they were allowed to exercise their authority under the Northwest Territories Act to borrow funds on the open market, instead of always from the Government of Canada. They would have to exercise their responsibilities well and in a manner which would enable them over a period of time to obtain the credit rating to which the special representative of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) referred. It is a process of learning how to manage their fiscal affairs.
Mr. Drury went on to say:
A more predictable level of general purpose grant would permit the executive member to anticipate additional revenue needs more effectively and to take the steps necessary to raise those revenues in a timely and responsible way. The level of federal financial support would become a "given" revenue item in the GNWT budget calculations rather than a residual supplementary item to balance the budget.
This is important. At the present time one must find out how much taxation one will receive from income tax, corporate taxes, the sale of licences, liquor profits and everything else. Then one must figure out the necessary expenditures, for example, how much it will cost to operate schools and hospitals, fill in potholes in the roads and everything else. Then the federal is asked to make up the difference. In my opinion it is unfair to both territorial authorities and to the federal government for the federal government to be always in the position of being asked to give as much as possible, and then a little finagling goes on. It would be better if some kind of formula arrangement could be made, as is the case with the provinces, wherein the territories could anticipate in advance the funding

March 29, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
which will come to them. At the same time the federal government would know how much money it would have to spend. We would get rid of the dog fights which occur every year when budgets are drawn up.
Mr. Drury continued:
An important measure of autonomy would be permitted that is not now available to the executive and the council, since it would be their responsibility to meet residual GNWT revenue needs.
This is important. It would make the territories act in a responsible manner because they could not overspend and then expect the federal government to make up the deficit. They would have to keep their affairs in order. He went on to say:
Future federal financial support should reflect not only federal responsibilities for an evolving territorial government but also the genuine fiscal need of the GNWT, consistent with the principles underlying the federal equalization program. The aim should be for equitable treatment of all Canadians, regardless of whether they are under provincial or territorial jurisdiction.
This is another important point. In that area of Canada we want the same type of treatment as people who make the provinces their home. If there is an equalization formula or program which operates for the provinces of Canada, why cannot this be extended to the territories? I admit that at this time, because of limited revenues in the territories, there would be need for additional financial assistance from the Government of Canada. All we need is one or two medium-scaled resource developments and then the financial picture would be reversed. This would be to the advantage of the federal government for having partaken of a program such as this.
The final quotation from the Drury report is as follows:
Federal-GNWT agreements for transfers of federal responsibilities should be negotiated that provide predictable GNWT funding levels. Funding should be in accordance with general guidelines agreed to between the two governments, taking into account the reduced claim on federal finances as a consequence of the responsibility transferred.
Then the important part read:
Any federal financial saving earmarked for the GNWT should be transferred to the inner cabinet budgetary envelope for fiscal transfers to the provinces and be included in the estimates of the Department of Finance.
The great problem of the territories now is the subvention of the Government of Canada. It does not come out of the envelope to which the special representative of the Prime Minister referred. It comes out of the budget and is carried in the estimates of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Anyone who has had anything to do with that department knows it is not a desirable situation. Transfers from the senior government to territorial governments should be carried in the same cabinet envelope as transfers to the provinces. It should be the responsibility of the Minister of Finance, not the responsibility of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro).
These things have been said many times in the past. Financial officials at the political level have come down from the Northwest Territories several times to make their case before committees of Parliament. The Minister of Finance came down about a year ago to speak on this very matter. When the parliamentary task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements visited the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, it was told very much the same thing. I am pleased that members of the task force listened carefully to what the two governments
had to say. Members went out of their way to discuss some of the problems in the report they prepared for Parliament.
I should like to read one quotation from the report entitled "Fiscal federalism in Canada" to illustrate that these people listened to the special concerns of this important part of the nation:
The task force believes that although federal territorial government fiscal arrangements based on a longer-term formula approach might appear to lessen accountability to Parliament in the short run, in fact, it could be increased in the longer term by coupling the periodic renegotiation of the new arrangements with a requirement for a specific report to Parliament on their effectiveness. Accountability would be further enhanced if there were to be a requirement for this report to be referred to a parliamentary committee for review and assessment.
In some ways I wish the parliamentary task force might have gone further and looked carefully at some of the recommendations of Mr. Drury, but in general it listened and seemed to have come to the same conclusions as Mr. Drury. I am sure anyone who looked carefully over a period of time at the problems relating to territorial-federal financing would also come to very much the same conclusions.
As we develop these fiscal arrangements, we should keep in mind that at some point in time the territories will attain provincial status. When that happens, we would want to have the same system there as in the rest of Canada. We must continually work toward that goal. It is interesting to note that the Yukon and that part of the Northwest Territories I have the privilege to represent, which is basically below the tree line or the District of Mackenzie, at the present time are as financially self-sufficient as some of the Atlantic provinces. When you take into account the public revenue generated and the public expense, they balance as well there as they do, for instance, in the provinces of Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island. We would hold though that the resources of the territories are such that if you develop only a limited amount of the potential, the revenue situation would be entirely reversed. The federal government would get back all of its investment in the north plus very much more.
So much for that which might have been taken as something of a digression, but it is an important subject. I have spoken on it before and I will continue to do so in the future. It is an evolving situation. We cannot deal with it once and then lay it aside. It will evolve over a period of many years and I look forwarding to addressing the House and giving updates on the accomplishments that we have made from time to time.
I will now return to Bill C-97. I know that the Minister of Finance has come under severe criticism for presenting this bill in its present form. My personal view of the bill before us is that it may not be that bad. I hate to have to say that, being a member of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, but certainly the bill has some things to recommend it. Some provisions are not as good as they might have been, but in general I think we can understand why the government has to take something of a tough stance with respect to transfers to the provinces.
March 29, 1982

The government is in very bad financial shape. This situation goes back over many years. Because of the economic policies followed years ago, we are now caught up in a situation where we have to pay for past excesses. We have lived beyond our means for some time and now we have to face up to the consequences of that. The government has to be very careful how it spends its rather limited resources. Therefore, there is some understanding, at least on my part, why the government has had to take a tack that some people regard as rather tough.
If I were to levy one criticism at the way the government has handled this affair, it is the way in which it has lacked a degree of honesty. Had the government explained the matter the way I have just done, the public might have had some sympathy, although I doubt whether it would be possible to have much sympathy for the mistakes of the past which have brought us to the present situation.
One of the ways the government has tried to get around the cutbacks that it is making is to issue press releases. I am referring specifically to a press release dated March 19 from "the office of the Hon. Allan J. MacEachen, Minister of Finance". If you read the first page of this communique, Mr. Speaker, what do you think it does? It stresses that payments to the provinces over the next five years will be $105.5 billion compared to $61.3 billion in the previous five years.
That is true, but that increase is accounted for by inflation, inflation caused by the government itself. What we have to do is to look at the formula that was used to come up with these figures and see what would have happened had we applied the old formula to the next five-year period. If we do that, we find that what has taken place is a cutback amounting to some $5.7 billion. That is the difference between what will be paid under the new formula and what would have been paid under the old formula. If we read through the communique, it does not make any reference to the amount of cutback; for instance, how much less the provinces will receive than what they would have received before. The situation is presented in the most positive light. I guess I can understand why the government operates that way, but in all honesty, the government is not honest. This is not an honest way to present that information to the House or to the people of Canada.
If we look at some of the provisions of Bill C-97, and I will try to go through them fairly quickly one at a time in order to give you my impression of them, the first item is sources of revenue to be equalized. I understand within Bill C-97 that the packet of provincial revenue is taken into account when you calculate the revenue which is to be equalized. This has been expanded by the inclusion of five or six new categories of provincial revenue. In general, I would applaud this move, and I think that most people who have spoken on this bill would see the effect of that as being from beneficial to neutral. The inclusion of certain resource revenue leaves one in a position of sort of not knowing which way to go. When you take into account the wasting nature of assets, such as mineral and oil and gas deposits, there is a necessity to treat that type of revenue differently from revenue which accrues on a continuing basis. From an oil field you can produce great revenue-on occasion, but only for a limited period of years.
Federal Transfers to Provinces
Most governments when drawing revenue from resources such as I have just described-and I am thinking of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta-have decided, and I agree with them, that a fair amount of that money has to be put into a fund, whether it is consolidated with a provincial consolidated revenue fund or set aside as a heritage fund, for reinvestment. It is capital rather than income. Therefore, when we start including resource-type revenue in provincial revenues used for the purpose of calculating payments to be made by the provinces-in other words, the equalization formula-we have to be very careful.
I would agree with the government that when it comes to the provincial component of the oil export charge, that is reasonable provincial revenue to use in the equalization formula. I do not think hon. members could argue that the oil export charge is a capital account item; it has to be treated as an income item. It is not a royalty as such but an export tax.
The five-province standard, which is to be used in place of the national average or the Ontario standard, would meet with my approval. It seems to make sense and I think it is one of the bill's provisions which has met with a reasonably wide degree of acceptance by members on all sides.
The payment floor and transitional guarantee also make sense and are non-controversial. The payment floor is not unlike the program which stabilizes provincial revenue. The provincial treasurer can forecast revenues and expenditures with a reasonable degree of accuracy. We would not want to see quantum leaps in the amount of moneys paid over because of the formula change, which would happen without some form of stabilization over the initial period. These things would also apply to the transitional guarantee and I am pleased to see provision for this in Bill C-97.
We then come to an item which may be a little bit more controversial, the payment ceiling. Everyone is agreed on the floor, but there is some difference of opinion with respect to the payment ceiling. The plan of the Minister of Finance is to tie maximum expenditures under Bill C-97 to increases in the GNP. As far as the minister is concerned, this is an effort to see that transfer payments do not escalate to ridiculously high levels. I know some of my colleagues might not agree with me, but in general I see the rationale for the payment ceiling. I think were I to be Minister of Finance, I would be inclined to do something similar. I know some provinces are going to squawk and scream over things like this, but because of the grave financial situation Canada finds itself in, it is in my opinion necessary to take some steps to see that expenditures just do not completely run away from us.
Federal government expenditures under C-97 will not be, by and large, blue book amounts. They will not come back to Parliament for approval; rather they will be statutory requirements for expenditures. It is therefore important that some cap be in place so that these matters do not get away from the

March 29, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
control of government and Parliament. I think, therefore, it behooves Parliament to look seriously at the minister's proposals to put a lid on this type of expenditure.
I have something to say about the population adjustment recovery payments which might get me into hot water with, for instance, the Premier of Newfoundland. I understand it is the government's intention to forgive repayment of amounts paid because population estimates under the existing formula were in error. Although I can see the need for something to cushion the effect this repayment would have on the provinces, I do not think we should wipe them off the board completely. Instead, I would favour allowing them to repay these amounts over a period of, I suggest, ten years. In addition, payment would be either interest free or at a very low rate of interest. I do not like the idea that we should bail everyone out of the difficulties in which they find themselves, albeit through no fault of their own, as in the case of an error in population estimates agreed to by both levels of government.
This will get me into trouble with the Premier of Alberta, but I also disagree with what that province did with respect to the indebtedness of certain municipalities. They had run up a lot of debt and found themselves in difficulty as far as repayment was concerned, and the Alberta government stepped in and said: "Okay, we are going to get the municipalities off the hook and pay off their debts". If you continually do that with a government at any level, it is very much the same as doing it with an individual; there is no incentive to be responsible in the future. One province will say that its neighbour ran up all these debts, got themselves into trouble and the federal government bailed them out; why shouldn't they do the same? Why should they run their financial affairs in a responsible manner when someone is going to come along and bail them out if they do not? Therefore, I wish the government had taken a little tougher stand with respect to the population adjustment recovery payments.
I wonder who else I can alienate during the course of this debate!

We now come to another rather controversial item, Mr. Speaker, the termination of the revenue guarantee. This is probably the most controversial item in the proposal now before us. Most of the cutbacks, if you are supporting the provinces, or savings in expenditures if you look at it from the federal government's point of view, will come from the termination of the revenue guarantee. This will amount to many billions of dollars over the next five years, so it is certainly worthy of debate. In fact, most of the debate on C-97 has been on this very point, and we have had great speeches by members on all sides defending the health care system and pointing out that if you terminate the revenue guarantee you are going to do all kinds of terrible things to the health of Canadians. The same thing applies to education. I have listened carefully to some of these arguments, and I prefer to deal with the technical and non-controversial aspects; in that way I will not get myself into so much trouble.
Let us look for a moment at the history of the revenue guarantee provisions of the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. I understand that this was introduced as a transitional measure in 1972. It was to expire in 1977. When 1977 came around, some of the old arguments were used again. In the enactments of that year, such as the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977, they were again renewed. The underlying idea was good! Because the formula was to be changed, because of the transfer of tax points to the provinces and the reduction of certain federal government expenditures, provinces could not quite calculate the effect. They were afraid that there would be a decrease in the amount of available money for health care, post-secondary education and other worth-while purposes. It was something akin to the flow of payment and transitional guarantees included in the present bill. It was for that reason that the revenue guarantees were included in the legislation of 1972 and of 1977.
To put it briefly and succinctly, my own thinking on this matter is that a deal is a deal.

If this deal is not working, we should look at the deal itself to see whether we should amend it, or to see whether there should be additional tax point transfers, or whether something is wrong with the EPF formula. I made some points with respect to the Northwest Territories and their dealings with the federal government. subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on this piece of legislation, Bill C-97, has reminded me of the parliamentary debate on a number of items over the last two years. However, in those debates and in the debates on this bill, we have not really demonstrated any attempt to come to grips with the realities of Canada today. Neither in legislation affecting the drastic economic situation Canada faces today, nor in legislation relating to federal-provincial relations, such as that which is before us right now, do we find any constructive leadership by this Liberal government.
In the economic field, the phrase "band-aid solution" has been often used, and appropriately, to describe every legislative measure or half-measure that the government has produced. The government's record in that very important field has been deplorable. However, that is not the subject of debate at this time. We are discussing a proposal by the government to alter, in a significant way, the federal government's financial assi-tance to the provinces. Both the equalization payments which are there to provide a basic level of services to all Canadians and the established programs financing legislation which assists provinces to maintain hospital and medicare services and university and community college programs are important to all Canadians. Indeed, equalization is so important that we have made it part of our new Constitution. Yet these legislative changes have been a result of inadequate discussion between the federal and provincial governments. If that were not bad enough, we in this House are being asked to pass, in all stages, the significant legislation which we saw for the first time on March 19.
I will deal with our role in this debate later on. However, for the next few minutes I would like to speak about the way the federal government continues to treat the provinces. Few will claim that the deteriorating relationship between our two senior levels of government can be entirely blamed on the federal government. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau is correct in claiming that some provinces are always kicking the federal government in the teeth. I would add that some provincial officials, as well as some federal politicians, seem to take delight in that type of behaviour. This provincial attitude has been counterproductive; but the federal Liberal government has done little to create a better climate for federal-provincial relations.
The Prime Minister has too often displayed quick wit and quick temper rather than the reasoned remarks that his personal motto should call for. By issuing a death certificate for co-operative federalism, he is only adding further fuel to the fires of regional suspicion and hatred. The sticks of that fire have been piled higher with each act of this government. The way the Constitution was dealt with, the approach to oil and gas legislation, the unilateral method of handling the question of the Crow rate and the sudden demise of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, have all
Federal Transfers to Provinces
augmented negative provincial feelings. These acts have created animosity by themselves. However, the attitude, the methods and the process employed by the federal government have produced the worst animosity. Other speeches in this debate and in previous debates have referred to the growth of Quebec and western separatism during this government's terms of office. The hostile feelings of those residents in Canada, plus others in Atlantic Canada and even in Ontario, toward the federal government demonstrates that the federal-provincial relations disputes have gone beyond being a continuing war of words, of different wills or of different personalities. Neither side appears to be willing to work toward a united Canada.
The Prime Minister declares that co-operative federalism is dead because he feels that he has been kicked in the teeth once too often. Provincial politicians are always going to the polls to fight the numerous onslaughts of the federal government. The federal government feels it must set up direct federal liaison offices in each province to increase federal visibility and that each cost-shared program must have a huge sign, preferably with neon lights, proclaiming that federal participation. At the same time, the provinces feel that they are being bombarded with federal ultimatums which dictate not only in federal areas of jurisdiction but also in any matter in which the federal government finds some belated interest. The federal government has been harshly treated by some provinces, but it has certainly given the provinces similar treatment.
In the bill before us today, the federal government has not really attempted to negotiate with the provinces. I find it ironic that when the federal government does not wish to act, it feels it must consult with the provinces. On the matter of freedom of information, it not only feels this need to consult, but it now believes the provincial and federal legislation must be uniform throughout this nation.
If freedom of information needs thorough consultation between the provinces and the federal government, Mr. Speaker, then certainly legislation affecting the ability of provinces to provide a uniform basic level of health care, postsecondary education and other essential services must require that same level of consultation.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) spoke on this legislation last Monday. I was in the House to listen to him. I read his speech in Hansard after that and I read it again on Sunday morning. I am certain that the minister has forgotten how to speak in everyday, understandable English. I looked at the bill before us, I read the reactions of some of the provincial governments, then I read his speech again. He is not using the English language to convey an explanation of this legislation. Instead, he uses the language to lead us away from the truth.
The Minister of Finance gives the impression that negotiations on this bill have been ongoing since October of 1980, when in that budget he said that "significant savings in social transfer payments" would occur. Yet later, he admits that

March 29, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
serious negotiations did not occur until after the November 12 budget of 1981. Even then he made major changes in February, 1982 and expected the provinces to agree within the same month.
Clearly, negotiations have not taken place in any real and substantial way. Some provinces have complained that the federal government's finance minister refused to meet with his provincial counterparts, from December 1980 to November 23, 1981, almost a full year, even though a meeting had been promised for as early as March, 1981. Clearly, if you do not meet you cannot discuss, and if you cannot discuss you cannot negotiate. This is not co-operative federalism in action; it is evasive federalism being acted out.
Negotiations are a sham when a proposal made to the provinces on February 4 for which documentation was not given to the provinces until February 19 is to be agreed to by the same provinces by the 22nd of that same month. They are given three days to respond to the federal government's position. It would take many more days for the provinces to be able to analyse the effect of the federal government's position.
The ultimatum negotiations of the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) where he demanded responses by March 3 with regard to funding proposals for post-secondary financing and, to a lesser degree, the fancy dancing of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) on the federal role in training programs also served to confuse the issue further.
There is no real need for this rushed and abortive attempt to negotiate with the provinces. As the hon. member from Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) mentioned last week, only the section of this bill dealing with equalization payments must be passed this month, even if only on an interim basis at this time. Those other sections where the majority of the dispute exists have no legislative deadline.
The effects of this legislation are not yet fully understood. Most provinces have not given their written reactions in the last couple of weeks. Most hon. members do not understand the legislation fully. We saw it for the first time on March 19 of this year. It would be irresponsible for us to pass this significant and important legislation without realizing all its implications.
I repeat that for established programs financing there is no legislative deadline. We are not forced to act on this section now. The federal government is giving itself a year to prepare for the start of new national guidelines for medical services and post-secondary educational services. Surely we and the provinces must have this information before we set limits on the federal level of funding for these important areas.
The minister in his speech last week spoke of a number of changes that are contained in this bill. He started by saying that there will be a "substantially changed fiscal equalization formula." Yet he wants to rush this bill through the House. The purpose of this section is to provide less money for the poorer provinces than they would receive if the present agreement were continued.
In addition, he spoke of moving to "modify established programs financing by eliminating compensation provided in exchange for the 1972 revenue guarantee." Those are his
words, not mine. Again this is a major change which we should not rush into. This also will drastically reduce funds the provinces are entitled to under the existing legislation.
One change the minister proposes is to forgive provinces which received an overpayment based on estimated population figures. However, Saskatchewan is not to be forgiven, while each of the other five provinces who received an overpayment will be forgiven. This bill specifically denies Saskatchewan this refund. Can we rush into legislation that is unequal in its treatment, on a retroactive basis, without first discussing the rationale for this proposed action? The amount is $50 million, and despite tales of new-found wealth in that province the amount is significant for a province of only one million people.
I do not wish to imply that all within this legislation is suspect; indeed, that is not the case. A provision extending for an indefinite period a fiscal stabilization program which protects provinces from a sharp downturn in revenues caused by a major slump in the economy and facilitating provincial borrowing in those periods is a good measure. A similar provision providing a revenue guarantee if the federal government makes substantial tax changes is also welcome. A section protecting provinces by providing 85 per cent, 90 per cent or 95 per cent of the previous years amount, depending on the provinces' per capita fiscal capacity, is also good. It gives protection against a rapid increase in a province's revenue in a one-year or two-year period.
The concept of including local governments' potential tax capacity also has merit. It will apparently roll $16.5 billion into the equalization standards, and it will more adequately reflect the revenue capacity of a province.
The provision of a ceiling where total equalization payments will be restrained by the growth in the GNP should provide protection for the federal treasury. However, its effect on poorer provinces if costs should escalate is something we should be discussing further in this House.
A very interesting new provision guarantees recipient provinces will have transitional payments for the next three years, guaranteeing, for example, that the 1982-83 equalization payments will increase by the average rate of income from 1977-78 to 1981-82. The federal Minister of Finance pointed out that in the next three years this transitional payment would mean an extra $165 million to the province of Manitoba alone. It is an admission on his part that the new proposals in this bill will drastically reduce the amounts provinces will receive under the present arrangement. Yet the minister says there are no cutbacks. If there are no cutbacks, why does he need a transitional payment scheme for the next three years? Why does the province of Manitoba receive $165 million over three years if there is no cutback? He is admitting that this legislation is giving him less money than the provinces would receive under the existing legislation. The Minister of Finance said that he agreed to transitional payments on the suggestion of the provinces, and in particular because of the arguments of the new government of Manitoba. That fact, in itself, is good,
March 29, 1982

but we must again ask ourselves why transitional payments are necessary if there are no cutbacks.
Under the present equalization formula, Manitoba should receive $452 million in 1982-83. Under the minister's new scheme, that province is entitled to $349 million, which represents a cutback of $113 million. With $82 million in transitional payments, Manitoba will receive $431 million, which is still $21 million less than they would have received under the present legislation. If we add the amount the province will lose under the new program for established programs financing to this $21 million figure, we find that the province will receive $62.9 million less next year than they would have received if the present legislation was continued.
Once the sugar coating provided by transitional payments is dissolved, it will be evident that the poorer provinces will be in a worse position. In 1986-87, the loss to Manitoba is estimated to be $248.6 million for one year alone. Yet Manitoba is not alone is this regard. The estimated cost for Newfoundland in 1986-87 is $30.3 million. For Nova Scotia it is $40.8 million. The figure for New Brunswick is $48.5 million. For Quebec, it is $1.22 billion. As I mentioned, the figure for Manitoba is $248.6 million.
Over the five-year term of this agreement the provinces will receive much less money than if the existing programs were allowed to continue. Again, I have figures relating to the same six provinces. The total federal cutback over the five-year term for Newfoundland is $90.3 million; $153.1 million for Nova Scotia; $172.7 million for New Brunswick; $3,960 billion for Quebec; and $828.3 million for Manitoba. Yet the Minister of Finance, in his unusual use of the English language, said last Monday; "I do not understand how the term 'cutback' can be applied to this particular program". We see billions of dollars in cutbacks yet he cannot understand how we on the opposition side, who are out there listening to people in the provinces, can use the term "cutback". The only argument the Liberals have used is that there is increased value in federal tax transfers, yet provincial tax increases will offset the shortfall in federal financing.
Let us review the true figures. Even after the federal tax transfers and the related increase in provincial taxes, the shortfall for some of these provinces is staggering. Again, I have figures for five provinces. For the next five-year term, Newfoundland, after removing the increased federal tax transfers and the provincial tax increases which are related to that, will lose $67 million. For the last year of the program it will lose $28.3 million. Nova Scotia, over the next five years, will lose $71.1 million and $27.8 million for the last year of the program. New Brunswick will lose $133.7 million over the five-year period and $42.5 million in the last year of the program. Quebec stands to lose $3,799 billion and in the last year alone, even after all the extra money which Liberal backbenchers have been talking about, it will lose $1,040 billion as a result of this new scheme. Over five years Manitoba will lose $719.3 million, and in the last year of the program it will lose $232.6 million. These figures are staggering but
Federal Transfers to Provinces
they must be put on the record because they represent the net loss faced by the provinces under this proposal.
The sugar coating effect of the transition payments may blunt the opposition to these measures. Already, some newspapers and politicians are looking only at the immediate result for 1982-83. However, the horrendous effects of this piece of legislation are only being delayed.
Those of us who are from the provinces concerned-Newfoundland, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Quebec and Manitoba-as well as those who are concerned about what result this legislation will have on the ability of the provinces to maintain a decent basic level of services, cannot support this bill. Liberal members who vote for the bill had better hope that the next federal election occurs before the sugar coating completely dissolves and Canadians discover what is being rushed through Parliament at this time.
The real question which must be debated right now is how the provinces, especially our poorer provinces, will be able to maintain existing programs at their present level when the federal government is taking away over $5 billion in the next five years. I remind hon. members that most of that money is being taken away from those provinces which are already receiving equalization payments, those provinces which we have agreed need the money the most.
When the Liberals refer to the resource rich provinces as the ones which will suffer under these proposals, they are obviously not telling the whole story. When the government complains that including all resource revenue of the richer provinces in equalization programs would create financial problems for the federal government, it is ignoring reality because for each of the last number of years resource revenue has been treated differently, and will continue to be treated differently simply by keeping Alberta off the list of the five provinces used to establish the equalization standard.
As provinces not receiving equalization payments, the major resource provinces are not adversely affected by the equalization proposals. They are not suffering from the cutbacks. They are affected by changes in the established programs financing through the removal of compensation for the revenue guarantee and, while it may be arguable that those provinces do not need federal assistance for hospitalization, medicare and postsecondary education, how does the federal government expect to enforce the federal standards, once they finally establish them, if they do not have a "carrot"-some way of controlling the activities of the governments of Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia? As I said earlier, my main concern is for developing provinces. While arguments about British Columbia or Alberta may be valid, they take attention away from those provinces which need the funds the most.
By referring to letters from the governments of the Atlantic provinces, the Minister of Finance implied that they support his scheme. In fact, those letters only support this proposal for a five-province standard for equalization over an earlier suggestion which he also made to restrict Ontario as the only province used for that national standard. That is the only point

March 29, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
those letters make and we should ensure that Canadians understand this. We should not let the Minister of Finance bamboozle us again. The Atlantic provinces do not support this scheme and he should not make that implication in his speeches.
1 remind Parliament that over 70 per cent of the cutback- and surely we can call it that, no matter what the Minister of Finance wishes-will be borne by those provinces with 44 per cent of the population and only 36 per cent of the national economic output. To hear some hon. members speak, we would assume that this is another measure by the Liberals to soak the rich. It is strange that every time the Liberals go out to soak the rich it is the poorer sections of Canadian society which are drowned.
My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill, mentioned that by a sleight-of-hand trick the Liberals have removed the compensation for the revenue guarantee and by doing so have made sure that the real increase in established programs financing is only 4.6 per cent instead of the 13 per cent the Liberals claim it is.
Parliament should be aware of what the all-party task force said about the level of federal funding. The task force stated on page 33 of its report:
-federal grants to provinces and municipalities expressed as a percentage of total federal spending have been fairly constant since 1970. There is, therefore, no ground to suggest that federal transfers have been getting out of control. In fact, they grew at a slower rate in the 1970s than they did in the 1960s.
What did the Economic Council of Canada say? It said that one should seriously doubt the wisdom and fairness of solving the federal deficit problem by merely transferring the problem to the provinces. The council went on to say that this is not a solution at all.
From where is the money for these programs to come? The federal government expects its own expenditures to increase by approximately 16 per cent this year. If the past is any tradition, they will probably increase by more. Are the provinces not expected to face similar increases, even without this drastic change in federal funding? Are the provinces going to tax their citizens more to maintain the level of services for medicare, hospitalization and post-secondary education? How are they supposed to know what they are supposed to finance? We have yet to see the guidelines for health care and post-secondary education. We are setting the funding limits now, and we are setting the guidelines for what should be a national standard one year down the road. Does that make sense?

speechtext: Of course not.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I think it is very likely that the standard of education and the standard of medical services in the less wealthy parts of this country will deteriorate. Why would the federal government propose a scheme whereby funding limits are established now and later we establish the federal standards and the federal guidelines?
For the last three years all parties in this House have expressed concern about the present level of services. By cutting the federal funding to which the provinces are entitled there can be no less pressure-and there certainly will be more pressure-on the level of services the provinces provide.
Did the all-party task force not state that money provided for the revenue guarantee should be treated as federal funding for health care and post-secondary education? If that is the case, why is the federal government, which had the majority on that all-party task force, eliminating this funding, and how could the so-called Breau report say one thing and the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) say the opposite in this House last Friday? Has he forgotten what his report is all about? Has he forgotten what the essence of that report was?
These are questions which should be asked and answered before we rush this legislation through Parliament. Today the state of federal-provincial relations is so strained that even Premiers like Howard Pawley of Manitoba, who really believes we should make co-operative federalism work, find it difficult to succeed. They find it very difficult because of the attitude of some of the premiers. They also find it difficult because of the attitude of the Prime Minister and some of his colleagues who sit opposite. This country needs a more positive attitude on the part of the provincial governments and on the part of the federal government toward each other.
Before this legislation becomes another thorn in the side of confederation, let us as members of Parliament make sure we know what we are passing. Let us ensure that no province suffers unnecessarily because of this legislation. Let us ask that guidelines for the level of services for health care and postsecondary education be established prior to limiting federal funding for those essential areas. Let us ensure that equalization payments really mean something and meet the needs of our less wealthy provinces and do not become another empty promise in our new Constitution. Let us insist that the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and the Secretary of State really negotiate with their provincial counterparts and not just play at consultations. Let us make sure that co-operative federalism really works and lives in Canada. For us to act in any other manner would not benefit those programs which we all believe to be very important and would not create a Canada where we are working together toward a better future for Canadians.
