subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the co-operative attitude of the hon. member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper).
I want to make only three comments about this bill. I am going to say a couple of things which have not been said before. First, I want to deal with the fund and join in the considerable discussion there has been about how much money goes into the fund and from where it comes. I want to make it abundantly clear that the governments of Alberta, past and present, have always stood very strongly and firmly for the principle of equalization. Albertans are part of Canada, and we agreed that social services such as health care and education should be provided at a reasonable minimum standard to all Canadians. As a matter of fact, it was strongly urged at the very beginning of the program by a former premier of Alberta that there should be equalization in Canada. Even though at that time Alberta was a have-not province, we felt it was necessary to make sure we shared anything we had. That has been typical of Albertans throughout the years. I remember that when 1 was a small boy during the depression years our family was as hungry as others. But that did not stop my mother, every time she baked, from sending a loaf of bread to another family who were also having a tough time.
Many times people are criticized for doing something good.
I remember being in El Salvador in 1965 representing the Canadian government through the Canadian Good Roads Association at the opening of the Pan-American highway. I also witnessed the opening of a hospital in El Salvador for which the Americans had paid. I travelled over the PanAmerican highway. The Americans had paid for 80 per cent of it, yet I did not hear one good word about the Americans from those people in El Salvador. All I heard was criticism, criticism, criticism. I asked the chap from Central America who was beside me, why? The Americans had built nearly the entire highway through Mexico to the United States; the Americans had built the hospital which was being opened, but they received no thanks for that. The chap beside me said that wherever there is a benefactor, there will be those who will hate that benefactor.
Sometimes I feel that way about the province of Alberta when I hear comments made in other parts of Canada. Albertans, the Alberta governments and previous Alberta governments have never asked for special concessions. They have shared with the rest of Canada in a number of ways. Mr. Speaker, I was hurt some time ago when I heard the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) say that Alberta did not want to share. I was even more hurt when I heard Senator Hays, a Liberal, say in a speech in Calgary that he was raised with oilmen and ranchers but now they do not want to share. I do not know where he has been living because sharing has been part and parcel of the every-day life of
Federal Transfers to Provinces
Albertans as, indeed, it has been of most Canadians. Who among us, from any province, would pass a youngster on the street who was hungry? Any of us would share our bread with him.
The equalization program which is now entrenched in the Constitution is a splendid thing. It ensures that all Canadians will have a minimum standard of social welfare, education and health. The higher we raise that minimum the greater the country will be. The weakest part of a chain is the weakest link and the weakest part of our confederation is the weakest province we have. We want to make sure that every province is strong and is given a chance to develop.
When I hear it said that Albertans do not share, I am upset because they have shared $18 billion in oil and gas revenues. I remember that when I was a member of the Alberta legislature I argued that we should have at least a two-price system for oil if not a three-price system. The first price would be the best one for the people who own the resource, the second would be the next lowest price for the people of Canada and the third would be the highest, or the world price for exported oil. Premier Lougheed replied that that is what the policy is, the fairest price possible, right across Canada and the highest price for people outside the country. By keeping the price lower than we needed to, we shared $18 billion with the people of Canada. I do not want any particular thanks for that, nor do the people of Alberta, but I think we should at least have recognition for it.
We also shared employment. I went to the tar sands plant at Fort McMurray when I was a member of the Alberta legislature where 2,000 people were employed separating the oil from the sand. A good half of them came from Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes and I was happy about that. I had dinner at a table where one person was from British Columbia, one was from Alberta, four were from Ontario, four from Quebec and two or three from the maritimes. Those people were helping develop the resource and that is the way it should be.
We also want to share in the fund. I want to be fair with the people of Alberta and I want the federal government to be fair with them when building the fund up. At one time we in Alberta argued-and the principle is sound-that revenue from non-renewable resources should not be part and parcel of the fund. A number of hon. members will probably disagree with me, and I respect that, but I argue that as we only have those non-renewable resources for a short period of time we should build for the day when they are not available. That is what the people of Alberta have been doing with the Alberta heritage trust fund; when the oil and gas is gone threre will be something there to lighten the load that the people will have to carry.
We argued that revenues from depleting resources should not form part of the fund, but we lost the argument. In the 1976 revision oil revenue was included and has formed part of the fund since. I still do not think the principle is sound,

Federal Transfers to Provinces
however. A non-renewable resource is a depleting resource and any province should have a chance to make use of the revenues which are only available for a short period.
My main reason for speaking today, Mr. Speaker, is the changes that have been made. Instead of "oil", there is now reference to "conventional new oil revenues", "conventional old oil revenues", "heavy oil revenues", "mined oil revenues", "domestically sold natural gas revenues" and "exported natural gas revenues". I think members of the committee should find out whether there is a fish hook in this which is designed to hurt Alberta. There are those who would like to do that. If there is a fish hook in this, it should be taken out. We will pay our share but let us not double the share simply because we have some non-renewable resources today.
Why did the minister change the provision from just oil and gas and make the various distinctions? The committee should examine this, as I shall at report stage, note the changes that have been made from what was contained in the old act. I want to know if there is a fish hook in this which is designed to hurt one province. I have seen that happen before, Mr. Speaker. I do not care whether it is little P.E.I. or big Ontario or big Alberta, no province should be discriminated against. Every province should be treated fairly and squarely. I make no apologies for that stand, Mr. Speaker.
There are three ways of sharing, namely, through the fund, and we are happy to do that, through employment and through a lower price for gas and oil for the people of Canada.
The third and last point I want to make concerns a reduction in services. When I was in the provincial legislature many programs were started by the federal government with a great blast of trumpets. Then suddenly the federal government dropped out and the province was left holding the bag. That is a very bad thing, no matter which party is in power in the federal government. If it is not going to maintain a program it should make it clear from the beginning.
I remember one program that was designed to help handicapped and retarded young people which was started in the Banff area. Many people worked very hard on it and volunteers gave their time to the project which was to enable retarded people who had previously drawn welfare to work and help maintain themselves. One learned to drive a car and started to earn a living, or at least part of his living, and others learned other things which would supplement their income and help them become self-sufficient. My heart thrilled at the happiness on their faces when they were able to say, "I am now making my own living." But after the third year when the program was going well, the federal government dropped out.
That is a bad policy and the same thing could happen with the established programs financing. The federal government will drop $5.7 billion over five years, or $1.14 billion every year if it is spread equally over the term. I cannot understand the mathematics of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), and neither could the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy). I do not know whether he was figuring in metric or what. Even in metric I cannot understand them.
March 29, 1982
When you take $5.7 billion away from the provinces, there must be a reduction some place.
The sad part is that established post-secondary educational programs will be affected; the quality of education will be reduced. I think hon. members opposite should realize that there will be less moneys for universities and colleges. This will either be made up by provincial governments or municipalities levying more taxes, or the fees of students will be increased. I read in a Montreal paper where one of its universities has now increased its fees for foreign students. Do we not want foreign students to come to Canada? Perhaps they should pay more than Canadians, but it is in our interest, if we are to share responsibility with the rest of the world, to raise the standard of education in Third World countries. It is very important for them to have educated people who can become leaders in their communities. Reducing the number who are coming to Canada does not work toward that objective.
One objective in terms of health was to have minimum health treatment for any Canadian who needed it. This is why Alberta gave up its medical program which was started by doctors. Alberta was doing fine under its doctors' program. It was an excellent program, but we were not helping other Canadians. Thus the government of Alberta said that it would drop out of its own plan and join the national program. Provinces that are not as well off as Alberta depend upon federal money. They will have to find money some place or lower the standard of health care. When provinces lower their standard of health care, it is more difficult for people to get into hospitals. It will even be more difficult for those who are poor. It will not affect those who are wealthy. As the hon. member for Churchill said, it is the poor who suffer, not the rich. The rich have enough money to attend universities, to have the best doctors or to do any of these things; there is no problem. The problem is with people who do not have money. This is why there is equalization. Any reduction hurts most in the provinces which need equalization. I plead with government backbenchers and cabinet ministers to ask themselves whether they want to be part and parcel of reducing the standards of the health and education systems in the country.
We should be raising the standard of education. The higher we raise it, the more we provide opportunity for young people to attend colleges, universities or various high schools. The better the country will be if opportunity is provided. Illiterate people in the Third World are having difficult times. Many people cannot read or write. They need opportunity. The same thing applies in our country where people are generally educated. That is not to say that we are well enough educated now. We should provide more opportunity for young people to attend colleges and universities and to learn trades so that they can contribute to the net worth of the country.
The effect of cutbacks on social services is an area which makes one's heart bleed. There are people who depend almost entirely on social services for their livelihood, for the education of their children, for the clothes on their backs. The provinces
March 29, 1982

or the municipalities will either have to cut back or raise taxes. If not, children will attend school poorly clad or fed.
I do not like to make personal references but I remember, during tough years, boys and girls who came to school without any breakfast. I remember boys and girls who came to school without any winter underwear in 40 below weather. One of my students rode a horse for five miles to school and he had no winter underwear. I asked him, "Where is your winter underwear?" He said, "My dad is a drunkard, we are on welfare, and they will not give us any winter underwear." After riding to school in 40 below weather, his skin was blue. I was so angry that as soon as school was out that day I drove to Drumheller and phoned the then premier of the province, Mr. Brownlee. He told me to talk to the minister of welfare. I phoned the minister of welfare and he said, "That is the rule; if the father drinks up his money we cannot help". This was during the depression years. I said, "Are you going to make the kid suffer because his father is a drunkard?" He said, "That is the rule". Then I phoned Premier Brownlee again and I told him the story. He listened and said, "That kid will get winter underwear". Three days later winter underwear was provided to the boys and girls of that family. I wondered whether this was the way government worked, that someone must fight for winter underwear. This is one of the reasons I am in politics; it is not my idea of government.
Government should help those who need it. People need help through established programs. The government should not be cutting $5.7 billion and telling the people that it is not reducing the equalization fund.
The hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) mentioned that he did not like the idea of the Alberta government giving $1 million to its municipalities because this action might make people irresponsible. 1 can understand people saying this if they do not know the real facts behind the so-called gift to municipalities. The municipalities of Alberta had debts which were not the result of recklessness on the part of their councillors. At one time I think I knew every municipal councillor in the province of Alberta, and I did not know one who was reckless. People who are that close to municipal governments must be careful, or it is not safe to walk down the streets. Day by day councillors rub shoulders with the people. One municipality had debt because sewer and water systems were required; another municipality wanted to be rid of dust which was causing lung trouble, so it paved the roads; and another municipality required a bridge. Some municipalities had no debt, some had a little and some had a lot.
How did the government of Alberta deal with the situation? It gave a per capita grant to all municipalities. Those with no debt were able to build up capital assets. Some of those with debt were able to wipe it out. Those with a little debt were able to provide other services to their people. Those with the biggest debt used most of the money to pay it off. It is another example of sharing provincial revenue with the municipalities. Municipalities are the creation of the provinces; why should the provinces not share their revenues with them? I am proud
Federal Transfers to Provinces
of the fact that the Alberta government provided help to the municipalities to eliminate their debt.
Also I say to the hon. member for Western Arctic that he should have seen the faces of the people in those municipalities when they were told that the debt was paid. It was similar to how I would feel if my father came to me and said, "Well, you have been a half decent guy; I will pay off your $2,000 debt". It would be a wonderful load off my shoulders. Many fathers do it. I do not think that is wrong, I think it is good. The more sharing we have in that way, the better. But remember, this money belonged to all Albertans. The province is simply passing the money on to the municipalities because all of it does not belong to the provincial government. There are principles there that are important and the same principles are important in this bill.
By all means, let us keep equalization. But at the same time, let us make sure that we are fair with each province. Let us make sure that no province is discriminated against in the building of the fund. Let us be fair to all provinces that receive the fund so that social services, education, and health care particularly, will at least reach a reasonable level of which any Canadian need not be ashamed.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am very happy to rise and address this bill because of its fundamental importance to our country, not just in the abstract but for Canadians as individuals. This bill is crucial because it will affect the day to day lives of all Canadians.
Bill C-97 deals with established programs financing and with equalization. It is a mixed bill. In that sense it is similar to the oil bill which caused all the kerfuffle which motivated the Conservatives to stop all business in this House. That bill was split eventually, and it is right that it was.
I feel that the bill before us should be split. Why do I say that? Quite simply because the government is trying to say that Bill C-97 has to get through the House now, that there is no time to be wasted if payments are to continue to the provinces. Therefore, this bill must go through now. In fact, the only part of this legislation that has to be dealt with quickly is the equalization portion of it. We could deal with the EPF portion of it over a much longer period of time. This raises the question why the Liberal government of the day is pushing this bill through the House so quickly, as it attempted to push the oil bill through. I must conclude that the government is doing this because it really does not want a full examination of the implications of the changes in fiscal transfers to the provinces.
We have all been able to make the point with regard to the established programs financing portion of this legislation and how that will have a detrimental effect on the provinces and all of our citizens. But the equalization part deserves full examination as well. By rushing this matter through Parliament, we will not have the time to understand fully the implications of

March 29, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
the changes in the equalization portion of this bill. The provinces will not fully understand the implications of the changes which the government is pushing through the House.
I am not surprised when the government of the day intends to push a legislative measure through the House quickly. But it does concern me when the official opposition, the Conservatives, who fought the oil bill vigorously and demonstrated their capacity to force the government to split a bill, is abandoning the fight when it comes to health and education. The official opposition has demonstrated its capacity to "stop Trudeau" from ramming an important measure through the House. Yet when it comes to fiscal transfer matters affecting health and education for all citizens, the official opposition does not exercise the same strength and power it has demonstrated it has. Why did the Tories not do that for this bill? Why do we not stop the government from rushing this bill through the House?

My colleague says oil before people.
This bill is an example of unilateral action. It is the federal government moving without the co-operation of the provinces. It is a demonstration of the fact that the government has completely abandoned the notion of co-operative federalism. It is really acting with a heavy and an arbitrary hand. It is not surprising the Liberals are doing this, but why are the Tories not fighting to stop this from happening? The Tories made a big issue of this when it came to the Constitution. They demonstrated their capacity to stop the government in this House. Yet when it come to the substance of confederation, which is the bread and butter of the financing that will help every family in Canada with regard to its health and education, the Tories are not here to carry on a real battle.
In the final analysis, I am not surprised that the Liberals and the Tories take the same approach to fiscal transfers. Fundamentally, they have the same economic strategy. They have the same approach when it comes to high interest rates, which continue to hurt people.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext:
Why is this an important issue? Why is Bill C-97 an important matter for this Parliament? Why should we be fighting it tooth and nail? Why should we be "stopping Trudeau" with regard to this unilateral action? We should be doing all of those things because the government, through this legislation, is reducing transfers to provinces for health and education, much needed social services, by the amount of $5.7 billion.
The government has eliminated the revenue guarantee. Previously, this was a guarantee for which the government took great pleasure in taking credit as a contribution to health and education services. Now when the government wants to get rid of it, it is claiming the guarantee has nothing to do with health and education. This bill to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act is a very significant one because it affects services in a crucial area that are available to all Canadians.
This bill is really an attack on medicare. The federal government is pulling out of medicare funding. The federal government is pulling back on its share of medicare expenditures.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: That is nonsense.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
At the same time the government is claiming that it wants strong national standards in health care. The government's action is to pull back on funding, yet its words are "Let's have high national standards".
I think most people will agree that actions speak louder than words and that this Liberal government, through the legislation before the House today, is attacking medicare. By cutting back on the funds available to the provinces for health care, the government is encouraging doctors to extra bill, thereby reducing accessibility to much needed health care in Canada. By this action the government is in fact promoting doctors' strikes because it is reducing the capacity of the provinces to pay for medical services at what doctors feel is a fair rate. It discourages investment and innovation in the health care system.
March 29, 1982

The preventive measure approach would mean lower costs in the long term, but it requires investment today in order to achieve those objectives. We need the financial wherewithal to establish community clinics. We must be able to experiment with salaries for physicians and not rely solely on the fee-for-service approach. We should be able to move into the area of prenatal and post-natal care. This would have long-term implications for the general health of the population and would reduce health care costs. We should have the funds to be able to experiment with new services for which there is a growing demand, such as home births, while keeping in mind that the infant death rate is much lower in those nations which combine supervised home-birth services along with hospital facilities for high-risk births, as compared with those countries which rely on hospitals only.
This legislation has very serious implications for us all and is a direct attack on medicare and health services. That, however, is not the only implication of this legislation. The Liberal government says it is not really cutting $5.7 billion in transfers. The minister said this was not really a cut. It is, he says, something more in the order of $1 billion because of the fact the government is transferring tax room to the provinces. In other words, the government is pulling out of a taxation field and the provinces will benefit thereby.
Well, let us examine that a little more closely. I ask the question, what tax room? Last November's budget did not lower taxes. It was in fact a real tax grab. Every Canadian knows that because everyone in this country has been hit and in some way hurt by the November budget.
There was a great hue and cry when the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) stood up in this House and said he was bringing equity to the taxation system, when in fact experience showed he was attempting to raise revenues and hurting everyone in this country. He reminds me very much of Colbert, finance minister to Louis XIV. Colbert said that the art of raising revenue was to pluck as many feathers from the goose with as little squawking as possible.
The problem with this minister is that he could not pull it off. There was squawking, and deservedly so. Everyone knows that the November budget raised taxes and in no way freed up any real taxation room for the provinces. The Minister of Finance, when he attempted this trick of plucking feathers from the goose, should have kept in mind that this is the twentieth century, not the seventeenth. Perhaps he will do so the next time he plays Colbert to Louis XIV.
What are the implications of these cutbacks? First of all, they force the provinces to raise taxes. In my own province of Manitoba, where a newly elected government is seeking to maintain these services, they will be forced to raise taxes unless this Liberal government shows some heart and provides adequate funding to the provinces. The province of Ontario faces a similar situation and their response to it is to cut services and increase user fees. Taking community colleges here in Ottawa as an example, it is well known that the Ontario government is following a policy of raising tuition fees at the same time as educational programs are being cut. We
Federal Transfers to Provinces
also know that over the last little while the Ontario government has been moving to a market system in the area of health care. They want hospitals to act as free enterprise institutions, and they have been cutting beds and even closing hospitals. The provinces are doing this because they are forced to as a result of the cuts in transfer payments by this government.
Another area threatened by these cuts is that of postsecondary education. I am sure all members of Parliament have been lobbied very vigorously by members of the Canadian Association of University Teachers over the last little while, and quite legitimately so. They particularly targeted those MPs with universities in their ridings. I met with them and they gave us documentation regarding the implication of these cuts for universities. As an example, they referred to the Avro Arrow. They indicated that by cutting such a technologically sophisticated program the government of the day hurt the economy. That was a good example because it occurred under the Conservative government. This illustrates once again that the Liberals and Conservatives follow fundamentally the same economic strategies and policies with regard to expenditures.
What are the results of these cuts? As far as the universities are concerned, it means larger classes, more impersonal student-teacher relationships, inferior equipment and poor library support for students. Buildings and equipment decay, there is a reduced research capacity and the use of underpaid and part-time teachers. There are new entrance barriers to women and native peoples. Highly competent people are leaving the universities. As an example, a graduate with a B.Sc. in engineering can get a greater income in the private sector than he can as a lecturer or assistant professor at a university. Therefore, what motivation is there for him to work in the university and produce the technically trained people needed to keep the economy strong?
The University of Ottawa delegation which met with me indicated they are hiring at the assistant professor level only. Now, we are not all experts in how universities are run, but they indicated to me that there are four levels of teaching, consisting of a lecturer, assistant professor, associate professor and a full professor. That is the sort of ladder of qualification. The university had been forced to hire at the lower level of assistant professor only. This means that the most highly qualified people are no longer in a position to be hired by universities, and this also means a reduction in the quality of university education. Of course, this affects morale in the universities, which is falling.
These are some very concrete results of this legislation and these cutbacks in transfer payments to the provinces as they affect universities. This indicates a general decline in the quality of universities, particularly since the late sixties and the early seventies when we were investing quite heavily in universities.
Since about 1977, while the quality of our universities has been falling because of the lack of adequate funding from the

March 29, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
federal government, the competitive strength of the Canadian economy has also been falling. The reason for this is quite obvious. Because we lose the capacity to produce highly trained technical people, we lose our competitive edge in the world market. These two trends, the decline in the standards of our universities and the decline in the competitive position of the Canadian economy, go side by side. It is time for the government to recognize the direction of this relationship and reverse it.
Another way in which post-secondary education in this country is threatened by these reductions in transfer payments is that for each and every one of us the costs of educating our children are going up. Not only are the costs of education going up, but we are buying cheapened education for our children. A friend of mine calculated what it will cost him to send his daughter to university next year. His four daughters go to university, and it will cost him $5,000 a year. 1 have three young children, and I must say that the cost of sending children to university deeply concerns me. These costs are rising because of the cutbacks in funding and rising tuition fees. There has been a cheapening of university education itself. How many families could really afford to send two or three children to university at today's price of $5,000 per child? Goodness knows what the price will be tomorrow or the day after.
As a result of these rising costs of education, universities will become less accessible. This will reinforce the inequalities in our society. It will mean that the gap between the poor and the affluent will continue to widen. Universities were once the symbol of hope of this nation for greater social and economic equality. They were once the symbol of hope of many young people who wanted to climb above poverty and become contributing members of society. By these kinds of cutbacks in transfer payments, we are making it less possible for universities to be a symbol of hope, both to the individual person and to society as a whole.
It is not just in the area of universities that we have a worsening condition. The federal government is certainly making public statements with regard to the pulling back of dollars for community colleges. The government indicates that it wants these dollars to go to the private sector instead, to the industries. I would note, quite frankly, that community colleges are provincially administered institutions. It seems to me that pulling money out of the community colleges and putting it directly into private sector firms shows that the real goal being pursued is not better training for people; rather, it is greater political visibility for the federal government of the day, with the clear objective of gaining more seats in this House for Liberal members.
Rather than playing this kind of partisan politics, playing with people's lives, the Liberal government, the government of the day, should begin a program of requiring industry to train people. Right now it simply uses what it calls incentives, but there is no program of mandatory training by industry itself. This could be done. We should remember that only a few days ago we became aware of the fact that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) is deliberately seeking
to hire some 20,000 to 25,000 skilled workers from abroad at a time when we have over one million unemployed.
Why is he seeking to hire these skilled workers from abroad? It must be because his training programs for skilled occupations in this country are a failure. One of the reasons they are a failure is that we do not make it mandatory for industry to train. We could do this by establishing a grant levy system. This would be a system that would require individual companies within an industry to pay into a fund. Those companies within industry which trained people for skilled occupations could draw from that fund in order to pay for that training. Therefore, rather than taking the approach of pulling money out of the community colleges to give to industry so that the government of the day could have greater political visibility, which is a partisan route, we should be dealing with the social reality. We should be seeking to establish training programs which really work. We could do that by making it mandatory for industry to train for skilled occupations. A system could be set up which would allow for that training to be financed industry-wide, not simply by each individual company.
In dealing with the threat that this bill represents for postsecondary education, I would like to come a little closer to home. I am thinking of my own community of Winnipeg or, if I may be so parochial, my riding of Winnipeg-St. James. I took the trouble to consult with two post-secondary educational institutions in my riding. I must say that I wished that the federal government had done the same thing. I have been asked by people from both institutions to put some of their concerns and views on the record. Perhaps if the federal government, before introducing this legislation to the House, had spoken to people in actual educational institutions, it would have come in with a different sort of legislation and with a different approach. I will specifically refer to the University of Winnipeg and then I will deal with the Red River Community College.
With regard to the University of Winnipeg, it is obvious that I cannot name the officials involved and I have no desire to do that. However, I want to state the feelings of the people involved in the administration and development of programs at the university, as they are key to the university. They quite clearly felt that the university had been underfunded by the previous provincial government, that previous provincial government being, of course, a Progressive Conservative government which was hardly progressive. They indicated that the present Manitoba government, under the cutbacks at the federal level, was offering very large grants to the university. I think it was in the order of a 16 per cent increase. This was being offered by a New Democratic government which was recently elected. The hopes of the people at the University of Winnipeg were that the federal government would cease this cutback approach and would take the route of offering adequate financial support to the provincial government so that the provincial government would be in a position to meet the full needs of the university community and, therefore, of the
March 29, 1982

City of Winnipeg. I am speaking on this issue today in order to express those hopes, because they must find expression some place and they certainly have not found expression on that side of the House.
The people to whom we spoke at the Red River Community College indicated, first, that they really appreciated the opportunity to express their views with regard to this legislation. That once again indicates the lack of consultation by the federal government with people who will be directly affected by the cutting back of funds. The Red River Community College's chief concern was with regard to rumours and implications that have been spread in the press that the community colleges are not doing their job, that somehow the community colleges are not training people for jobs that really exist and are somehow off target.
The people from the universities and colleges can be concerned, but obviously the people who were spreading these notions in the press were political; in fact, they were Liberal political people, members of the present government and cabinet. They were spreading the notion that somehow community colleges were not on target when it came to training people.
The record is quite different. The record shows that despite the fact that we have a slow economic situation right now, the graduates of community colleges have been able to find jobs. A survey conducted last summer by the Manitoba department of labour and manpower shows that 85.9 per cent of the 1980 graduates of the province's three community colleges and of the community college division of St. Boniface College have found jobs. In a tight economy it is very important that community colleges remain responsive to the job market, and the survey with regard to the graduates of the community colleges indicates that those people had found jobs.
I would note specifically that 88.4 per cent of those with jobs had remained in the province. So they did not have to run half-way across the country to find jobs; they found those jobs at home right where they were trained. And 82.7 of those with jobs found jobs related to the field of training. They not only found jobs but jobs for which they were trained. Most of the graduates found their first jobs within five weeks. So they were not hanging around for six months or a year to find a job; they found a job very quickly.
The graduates of Red River College in Winnipeg represent only 2.5 per cent of the unemployment rate among community colleges in Manitoba. In Assiniboine Community College it is zero per cent. These rates are so much lower than the general rate within the community that it indicates how well the community colleges are doing in terms of training people for jobs that exist. They are doing a good job in that way. So that the notion that is being spread by the Minister of Employment and Immigration that the community colleges are not doing their jobs, or are off target and therefore the money should go into private industry, is false.
If we wanted to, we could improve the record of community colleges, in terms of their training of people, by implementing
Federal Transfers to Provinces
the system of predicting what jobs are going to be available. That is a system proposed by the Canadian Labour Congress. It is a system which will allow for the collection of information from industry about investment plans and resulting job opportunities on a confidential basis. If we want to improve further the capacity of community colleges to be on target with regard to their training, we can do that, rather than going the cheap political route of simply taking moneys from institutions that are provincially administered and putting it into private industry because of the political, visibility.
I wanted to get on record, Mr. Speaker, the concern that some of the local training institutions in my community have with regard to the real cutbacks in funding that are going on and are being promoted by this government.
I want to make another major point, on a more broad level, with regard to the transfers of money from the federal government to the provincial governments. Manitoba is hit very hard. In fact, the province of Manitoba is hit harder than any other province. This is illustrated both by statistics from federal government documents as well as by statistics put out by the provinces themselves. I will give an example.
Over a period of a number of years, five years, on the average the over-all funding for all provinces will go up by 69.8 per cent, whereas for Manitoba it will go up by only 37.2 per cent. So there is a real difference in the way that the provinces are affected. Manitoba, of all the provinces in the country, is hit hardest by these cutbacks. The Province stands out, and I wonder whether this was because, when there was a premier who simply engaged in fed-bashing, this was some attempt to punish that premier for his activity. If that is the reason, I hope the federal government would realize that that premier is no longer the premier of Manitoba.
Common justice would call for some rectification of the over-all impact among the provinces. Why should Manitoba be singled out to be hurt the most by these cutbacks? The federal government should not be brutal. New Democrats in Manitoba will not engage in fed-bashing; we will tell it like it is. Unless there are real changes in these transfers so that Manitoba is treated justly, we will speak out.
As well, this raises some curious questions. Why bother to have a Liberal in this Parliament? We have from Manitoba two Liberal members. We have a Liberal federal cabinet minister from Manitoba. Why does he have no clout in cabinet? How can they justify the fact that Manitoba can be so hard hit? Is it because we have a Liberal cabinet minister? No other province has been hit so hard. It is time to change this formula, to change this transfer payment in a way that will mean that Manitoba is treated fairly with regard to these overall transfer payments.
Over all, Mr. Speaker, what seems to be happening, as I see it, is that the two provinces that are really getting hard hit are Quebec and Manitoba. By observing the figures I have come to this conclusion, that the federal government is really hurting the two have-not provinces that are in the middle. The provinces that are at the bottom, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, are being hurt; but

March 29, 1982
Adjournment Motion
those in the middle, that are closer to the national average in terms of wealth, are being hit harder. That is because the cutbacks in transfer payments are reducing the number of have-not provinces almost by fiat, in order to save federal government revenues.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, this legislation should not go through this House, for some very simple and fundamental reasons. The legislation represents an attack on medicare as a universal system of health care. It is forcing provinces to raise taxes. It is hurting the have-not provinces, in particular Quebec and Manitoba. Certainly it is hurting Manitoba more than any other province. You do not have to seek my advice in regard to this matter, Mr. Speaker. The parliamentary Task Force on Federal-Provincial Fiscal Relations said no to cutbacks in fiscal transfers in the sections of health, postsecondary education and social services. The Economic Council of Canada said no to cutbacks as they affect postsecondary education and health care.
So, Mr. Speaker, I wish that the government would come to its senses-although I hold out no hope of that happening- and stop the cutbacks, adopt a sensible economic strategy, create the wealth that we need to continue the services that we need in this country and bring some sanity back to policies in the federal-provincial relations arena.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. MacEachen that Bill C-97, to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977, and to provide for payments to certain provinces, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since it is getting late I shall be brief and keep the details for the debate on third reading. According to the members of the opposition, we on this side are talking about cutbacks, and the federal government is supposed to be reducing transfers to the provinces. I feel that they are leaving out part of this mental exercise, which is: how do we assess the federal transfers to the provinces over time?
First of all, how did the transfers start? In 1958, the federal government introduced the hospital insurance program and it was understood with the provinces that it would be a 50-50 shared-cost program. In 1957, a similar program was established for post-secondary education, and in 1968, the shared-cost format was extended to the health sector under a new program, commonly referred to as Medicare. The arrangements were renewed every five years, both for the three established programs and for fiscal equalization. In 1972, we renegotiated the arrangements for 1972-77, and at that time the concept of revenue guarantee was introduced, following the 1971 tax reform. Because the provinces, it was felt at the time, were suffering a loss of revenue as a result of the tax reform, the federal government agreed to compensate them for loss of revenue over the period from 1972 to 1977. In 1977, during negotiations for the period from 1977 to 1982, the federal government was being urged by the provinces to continue the process of decentralization that had been initiated, and it agreed to release the provinces from the obligation to have their accounts and expenditures audited, and approved so-called block funding or established programs financing. At the time, we decided that the federal government would finance 50 per cent of the real cost of expenditures incurred in the three programs during 1976 and that increases for subsequent years would be related to the average GNP growth over the last three years. Finally, we put another sum on the table, while maintaining this obsolete concept which had become totally meaningless, that is, revenue guarantee.
The fiscal arrangements committee did, in fact, make a thorough study of all these negotiations, and when I hear our colleagues on the opposite side, especially those belonging to
March 29, 1982

the New Democratic Party, say that the committee did not recommend any cutbacks, I feel I should read two paragraphs where all committee members were in agreement. The paragraphs appear on page 36, and I quote:
What is undeniable is that the federal government faces a major budgetary problem in the size of the public debt and corresponding debt service charges. In exercising its unique responsibility for stabilization policy in the post-OPEC period, the federal government-in common with most national governments in the western industralized world-took on massive deficits. Over the remainder of the 1970s, these deficits accumulated to the point where debt service charges now represent 20 per cent of the federal budget, and this share, which is a completely non-discretionary expenditure, is rising.
Thus the task force considers that the concept of fiscal imbalance requires a careful distinction between a structural problem in the design of the arrangements of confederation, and a problem of budgetary imbalance reflecting political judgements on revenue and expenditure priorities. The federal government is at an interesting intermediate point on the spectrum between these two extremes, a point where a prolonged cyclical budget deficit begins to lead to some aspects of a persistent structural imbalance. The structural problem emerges because the size of the debt accumulated to date begins to constrain to an unacceptable degree the margin of manoeuvre in federal government decisions on fiscal policy.
It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that all members of the fiscal arrangements committee recognized the constraints on the federal government's margin of manoeuvre at the time, before the MacEachen budget was brought down in November. The seven committee members also clearly recognized that the amount transferred by the federal government to the provinces and referred to as revenue guarantee, as my colleague from Manitoba pointed out with a smile, that none of the provinces ever spent this money on the program, not even the socialist governments we met. None of the provinces applied these amounts to their health or post-secondary education programs, not one. They built roads, they paid for all sorts of things, including patronage, but they never spent the money on established programs, and our colleagues recognized the budgetary and financial constraints with which the federal government had to cope. And now, because we are making reductions-and this represents 6.2 per cent of the total transfers for the three programs-because we are making reductions in amounts that were not being spent on the programs anyway, they say we are cutting back and that we are going to bring about a reduction in essential services and cuts in post-secondary education programs. Mr. Speaker, that is not true, because first of all, since the report was tabled, we have had a budget that is giving the provinces $685 million more per year. So we can subtract $685 million from the cutbacks of $1.2 billion referred to by our friends opposite, and it is quite true that at least the provinces will be able to do what they like with this money.
And what is the situation today in 1982? The fact is, the federal government is paying about 60 per cent of total costs incurred for health and post-secondary education programs. So, Mr. Speaker, I think that members who have been seeing or listening to certain lobby groups should ask the same people
Federal Transfers to Provinces
who are pressuring us to spend more money on these programs, to put the pressure on the provinces instead of on us.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, the concept of revenue guarantee is totally obsolete, because today, the provinces are receiving, not only as a result of the last MacEachen budget but also as a result of new Canadian tax measures, more than they would have if there had been no tax reforms in 1971. It is a little like someone who has a winning ticket and stands to get a certain sum of money for five years, and, when there is no money left at the beginning of the sixth year, starts complaining that society is treating him unfairly.
Mr. Speaker, our friends on the opposite side are talking about cubtacks, but the truth of the matter is that next year, federal transfers to the provinces under these programs will be increasing 6 per cent, rising to an average of 12 per cent during the following four years. That is all I have to say about established programs, since I shall be discussing this aspect in greater detail on third reading.
As far as fiscal equalization payments are concerned, from 1977 to 1982, the federal government paid $61 billion, and from 1982 to 1987, it will be transferring $104 billion. Here again, equalization payments will increase at a rate of 12 per cent annually, including the first year. I really do not know what kind of arithmetic or mathematical or metric or whatever system these people are using to calculate the figures I have here, Mr. Speaker, but in my book, when transfers are being increased at a rate of 12 per cent a year, how can you call this a reduction in the amounts being offered by the federal government?
As far as my own province, the province of Quebec, is concerned, it will continue to receive about one third of total transfers. In terms of equalization payments, in previous years, for instance last year, Quebec received $4.1 billion and this year it received $4.7. And then Mr. Parizeau comes and tells us that transfer payments to Quebec are being reduced. Mr. Speaker, that is a lot of hot air, and I feel provincial governments should first put their own administrative house in order and balance their own budgets before they criticize federal transfer payments, which are actually going up.
