subtopic: FARM CREDIT ACT FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT

speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-88, respecting loans to farmers, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

subtopic: FARM CREDIT ACT FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
That Bill C-88, respecting loans to farmers, be amended in Clause 8 by adding immediately after line 31 at page 4 the following:
"(1.1) For greater certainty, the expression 'bonds' referred to in subsection
(I) includes 'small business development bond'."
He said: Mr. Speaker, Parliament has allowed these amendments to the Farm Credit Act to go through second reading. They have been through committee and now they are at the report stage. I do not intend to repeat tonight the great value this act has been to farmers in the last 20-odd years, as I think almost everyone in the House must be aware of that fact. I agree completely with the minister when he says that the future of agriculture is ahead of us, with the world demanding so much of what we can produce from our land, water and air. It is absolutely essential that we have enough capital and the borrowing power of the nation to push forward this winning type of industry, agriculture, to make certain that we do not fail, and that the expansion of this industry continues.
March 29, 1982

When I talk about the expansion of industry, I think the minister is aware that what I am talking about is not just agriculture as we have known it, but agriculture of an altogether new type; intensive agriculture whereby we produce so much more from the same amount of land and utilize it in many different ways. I do not intend to elaborate on that. 1 think it is new to many people, but it is not new to the people looking at the future of agriculture.
These amendments which we have already dealt with at second reading and in committee are mostly housekeeping. They are useful housekeeping amendments. However, there is one amendment I mentioned at second reading debate and I want to put it on the record again so that it is clear. In my experience, it is almost a miracle the minister was able to get this amendment into the legislation. I am saying this clearly and deliberately because it is very important for us in Parliament to fulfil our obligations to the agricultural industry. We have to make certain that the agricultural industry has access to sufficient capital at low enough interest rates to make development possible.
1 shall read the section again so that the record of what I say now is complete. Hon. members have heard the amendment at report stage which I have just moved, through you, Mr. Speaker. I shall now read the section of the act I want to amend. This is Section 13(1) in the act, and is the eighth amendment in the bill. I hope every member and every person within the sound of my voice hears this amendment. What it says is revolutionary. It reads as follows:
The corporation may, with the approval of the Minister of Finance, borrow money by any means, including issuing and selling bonds, debentures, notes and other evidences of indebtedness of the corporation.
Why is that so revolutionary? Because for the first time the Farm Credit Corporation can be weaned of dependency on the Consolidated Revenue Fund. In the past, when we needed to put more money into the agricultural sector of the country through the FCC, we had to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) if we could increase the capital, and then borrow the money to lend to farmers. At the present stage of federal government finances, by any ordinary measurement, the government has to be considered bankrupt, if the ratio of debt to assets is considered, yet we have for the first time to my knowledge an agency of the Crown, the FCC, able to go out and borrow money by any means, and from any source in order to assist farmers to carry out their function. That part of the clause, "by any means" is the main subject of my remarks tonight.
I have congratulated the minister for being able to get that clause in. It bears out the statement he made last year after we on this side of the House made a series of proposals on how to get more money into the agricultural industry. The minister will remember that one proposal was to use the FCC as a type of bank and let all sources of capital lend money to it. Prior to this it was mainly the Consolidated Revenue Fund which provided the money. It could in theory borrow money, but now we have it laid down; it can borrow "by any means".
Farm Loans
Tonight I have moved an amendment which says, in effect, that what I have just described as possible, "by any means", should be clarified by a simple amendment in the Queen's English so no one can misunderstand it. The amendment as it appears in the Order Paper says:
For greater certainty, the expression "bonds" referred to in subsection (1) includes "Small Business Development Bond".
In the bill which amends the act it says:
The corporation may-
It says "may" not "shall":
-with the approval of the Minister of Finance, borrow money by any means-
It mentions bonds in general.
Why, then, do I put so much emphasis on this amendment? I want to describe my bitter experience, and I imagine most people in this House will have sympathy. I have mentioned already that we would like the principle of the small business development bond stated in clear English in this amendment so that those who draft regulations and get them approved cannot overlook that principle. Why is that so important? I, like others such as the hon. member for Moose Jaw(Mr. Neil), proposed some time ago that we use the FCC under this clause to provide income-averaging annuity contracts to individuals across Canada. If the Minister of Finance is going to throw that out of the budget, we will put it right back into the farm legislation, because it would attract capital to the FCC.
The bill has another important part which has a bearing on what I am going to talk about. The capital of the corporation has been raised from $150 million to $225 million. That is only important if you realize that under the Farm Credit Act for every dollar of capital you are allowed to lend $25. When this bill proposes to add $75 million to the corporation's capital, it really means that the FCC will now be able to lend roughly an additional $2 billion at any given time. That is a substantial amount of money, so the FCC must have access to the money in order to lend it out.
We all recognize that the Minister of Finance cannot even begin to provide $2 billion. He has enough trouble already with this huge deficit, and he has gone out on behalf of the government and borrowed money at 19.5 per cent. He is not going to dole that out in large amounts to farmers or to anyone else. The facts are very simple: since the government does not have the money, how fortunate it is that this bill will give the right to the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow money from other sources, by any means.
Here comes the crunch. Mr. Speaker, you and I are not lawyers. All my life when it comes to running government I have had to fight lawyers. These fellows are highly trained, ten times smarter than I am, and they come along and undo everything I want done. They are not going to distinguish between me-they had their crack at me 20 years ago-and the present minister. Their function in life is to put into words things that you think mean so and so, but in practice can mean something else.
I speak with great feeling on this subject. When I look back over all the mistakes I have made, both in administration and

March 29, 1982
Farm Loans
putting legislation into effect, in nearly every case they occurred because I allowed myself to be talked into something by a fast talking lawyer. When you look at this bill, Mr. Speaker, and you see that it says the corporation can borrow money "by any means", you will look then ask what that means? The lawyers will say it means anything you want it to mean. We are all lawyers here and "by any means" means "by any means"; that is plain English. However, the catch is the word "may". That word "may" is what undoes it all. Therefore, I would like to put on record things which have actually happened in the House over the last 25 years which will prove my point, that we should be careful whenever we see the word "may" in a section, when put there by legal draftsmen who say that "may" covers everything, including "by any means".
What are the facts? In 1959 I had something to do with drafting the new type of legislation dealing with the National Energy Board. Weeks and weeks of time were devoted by the legislative committee to dealing with just one of the sections. It stated that the board being set up "may" make recommendations, present new ideas and report to government. I said, "you may do it". I was a minister. I wanted the word "shall" put in: "The National Energy Board shall recommend and propose and warn the government". We had just gone through a disastrous ten years dealing with these large American companies coming in and taking over our energy industry. I did not want to repeat those mistakes. I wanted the best board we could get to keep the government informed of what was going on. I wanted that word "shall".
The beautiful and charming people who advised the ministers, with all of their law degrees and fast talk, said, "It is not necessary to put the word 'shall' in as 'may' will cover everything you could possibly wish or want". How could an ordinary minister or politician cope with this charm and elegance? It went through, and that was in 1959. I give this warning in all seriousness to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan).
In 1972, I asked the National Energy Board, through a committee of this House, why it had not carried out its function of recommending as laid down in the act. The board had two functions. One was its judicial and administrative function and the other was to recommend and keep the government informed. Its answer was that there did not seem to be too much approval from government colleagues. They did not want advice. I thought it was a great triumph when I got the new chairman of the board to agree, in committee, that he would do all he could to carry out this second function of the National Energy Board and tell the government what was going on. What was the result?
The Department of Energy, Mines and Resources which was formerly the department of mines and technical surveys, had its title changed a couple of times. The minister in charge of that department took the information put before him by his own department, information gathered from all the companies operating in North America and around the world, and he went out and said, "There is enough oil and gas in Canada to
last us for hundreds of years, if not a thousand years". He was not a dishonest man. He was a normal, little, country lawyer from Arnprior who believed the information that was put before him.
Then you should have heard all the clowns laugh. They said, "The man does not know what he is talking about. We have no oil. We have no gas. We are going to run out." All the turkeys and the chickens were running in all directions and we had this fraudulent national energy crisis. They said: "Break the Constitution", and they did. We were in an emergency. The government wanted to smash through the Constitution and take away the power from the provinces. Sure, they covered it up with nice words: "We are going to share with these people in Alberta, B.C., and Saskatchewan." The politicians got so frightened, because they had nothing before them except this report which came from the oil companies, that they panicked. So we broke the Constitution. Then it became popular to say that we had no oil or gas and that we were in an emergency, a crisis. Even the Supreme Court judges ruled that there was an emergency. When the leaves were falling on the chickens' heads, they ran around and told the whole world the sky was falling, and even the Supreme Court believed it.
What is the truth concerning energy? This is the year 1982. All the people in the world have a surplus of gas, a surplus of oil, a surplus of every type of energy. We did not know the facts soon enough. The National Energy Board, a few competent people, systematically and carefully worked year after year to discover the real situation. The minister who gave the prognostication of the future is dead. The sad part of the matter is that he went to his death with everyone thinking he was a fool because he said there was energy in this country for a thousand years. The truth is that he was not a fool. The truth is that there is energy for a thousand years-much more energy in this country than we know about. We do not even have a group of people in Canada today who have enough confidence to tell us the energy future. All we know is that the supply is many times, thousands of times, greater than what we imagined 20 years, or even ten years ago. We have the expertise.
Governments all over the world are looking to the skies and the whole universe trying to find access to energy when the stuff is right here. Look at the work we are doing on fusion energy. We targeted fusion energy for the year 2020. We are ahead of schedule. It looks like we will be there ten years ahead of schedule, But these are expensive forms of energy. The ordinary stuff is all around. I am simply using that as an example.
No parliamentarian or minister in his right mind should ever let lawyers get away with that word "may" when Parliament means "shall". I am trying to clarify, for the protection of all politicians, that when we must deal with legislation, let us learn from our mistakes. I am not saying that this matter on farm credit is as vital to the health of the nation as knowing something about the energy situation. I am simply saying, now that we have learned from bitter experience, we should not
March 29, 1982

prohibit a group of people from getting together to do the job they were supposed to do because we used the word "may".
To use another phrase, if I may say so, civil servants have learned from bitter experience that one must never make a mistake. The only way one can be sure of not making a mistake is to never do anything. They have a name for that. When one does make a mistake, they say, "CYA". Hon. members know that the first two words are "Cover your", and I will let hon. members decide what the "A" means. Let us not make the same mistake in this particular bill by inserting the word "may". Let us put in a few sharp definitions that even the lawyers and the people who draft the regulations cannot get around. We want to let them know, without any fooling around, what Parliament wants them to do. We are backing up the minister and making use of this legislation.
I do not know how many examples I will use here, but I can deal with this very quickly. Most hon. members in this House who have been here since 1972 or 1973 know that we passed a bill, supported by all parties, which stated that any child under the age of 16 could receive family allowance regardless of the financial circumstances of the parents. Whether the parents were millionaires or paupers, a child up to the age of 16 could receive family allowance. A child who went to school could receive family allowance up to the age of 18 without regard to the wealth of the parents.
That is what parliament did unanimously nearly ten years ago. Here we sit in 1982 and know, or some of us know, that orphans are not accepted, that teenage girls who get pregnant are not accepted. Parliament put nothing in there about discriminating against orphans; Parliament put nothing in there about discriminating against teenage girls who get pregnant. That is the time they need the help when they are going to school. Yet that crime is laid at our doorstep here in the House.
I feel sorry for a minister who has to stand, like that minister who said a few days ago that she should take it up with her colleagues on the Treasury Board, or whatever group she was in or in some committee, because that is where the discrimination against orphans exists, but they could not do anything about it as they did not have any money. As soon as they get the money she says they will do something about it. The blame for that does not lie with the ministers alone; it lies with us as Members of Parliament, knowing that this is happening over and over again, because experts on legal language draft our legislation, make these mistakes, and we cannot see through it. Things can be done over and over again through regulations that turn our ideas all around. Therefore, I make an appeal to all parliamentarians to be kind to ministers.
When we have a chance like this to propose an amendment that does have so much potential, let us make sure no one unpsets it in the drafting of regulations which are then put before Treasury Board, cleared there, and resulting in an order in council. We all know about the machinery and how difficult it is to look at everything carefully. How I would hate to see
Farm Loans
this very good piece of legislation reduced by the power to make regulations which interpret the words "borrow money" to mean "borrow at the market rate".
We have all sorts of devices for getting money below the market rate. What is the Small Business Development Bond? I do not mean the Small Business Development Bond as talked about in the budget, I mean the Small Business Development Bond principle, which says that if you lend money for a worthwhile purpose to such and such an agency, you are not to be taxed on your income from that loan.
If I lend $1,000 on the principle of the Small Business Development Bond to the Farm Credit Corporation, I know this will only give me 8 per cent on my money. That is just as good to me as lending it out on the market at 16 per cent, because I know I will not be taxed. We have had this principle in Canada since the First World War. It is used extensively and continuously in many states of the American union, and it has been used since 1979 through the Small Business Development Bond under the Income Tax Act.
Let us put in clear-cut English what this bond means, and that it includes any other type of bond. Then, if people want to lend their money on the principle of the Small Business Development Bond, they will know they will not have to pay tax on their income from that bond. They are then quite willing to accept half the dollar interest rate because they know they will not be taxed.
The Farm Credit Corporation will be able to act just like a bank, getting its money not only from farmers but from anyone who wants to lend at half interest rates. The corporation can then turn it over to farmers at roughly the same rate; a half per cent or one per cent more.
I cannot say that this measure will answer all the problems, but I almost guarantee that the minister will have access to millions of dollars in this way, making his life a lot happier; much happier than if he had to rely on a few million dollars from the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
I am not going to bother giving the other example I had, Mr. Speaker, because this matter was settled to my satisfaction some years ago. Parliament decreed that we should not tax other governments or municipalities which are spending money for worth-while purposes, like education, building roads, and so on: yet we have regulations in effect in Canada under which we tax municipalities who are spending money on vehicles for educational purposes. Parliament never meant that, but we went on, because we were slaphappy in the way we drafted the legislation, accepting the word of the lawyers that "may" will cover everything. That is not learning from our mistakes.
In conclusion, I made my case on second reading that the principle of the Small Business Development Bond should be used where the word "bonds" appears. Latterly, I sought legal advice from the House and from other sources as to what was necessary, and in every case I was told the language was clear enough; that the minister "may", or the corporation "may",

March 29, 1982
Farm Loans
borrow by any means-that you do not need any more clarification. I say I was fooled by that type of language before and I am not going to be fooled again. Draft me a regulation which will make it absolutely certain that they will consider the principle of the Small Business Development Bond.
The amendment you have before you does not quite say it like that. It says, "for greater certainty", and there are many precedents for that type of thing in our legislation, "the exression 'bond' referred to in subsection (1) includes Small Business Development Bond." What I mean there, and I want this to be written into the record so it will be just like the legislation, is that it refers to the principle of the Small Business Development Bond. I do not know any other way of writing it except the way I say it here.
The principle is clear. It is not the principle of the November 12 budget, which said that Small Business Development Bonds would only be given to persons in dire straits or in business difficulties. I want them available to any person on the simple principle that when you are investing your money in worth-while social purposes you will be glad to do it at half the interest rates as long as you know that the money is passed on at half interest rates.
This may be considered redundant by the lawyers, but I am asking Parliament to put its foot down and back up the minister. Give him his clauses as they are here. "For greater certainty" means just this. I wish some of my colleagues even on the government side would stand up and make an amendment that income-averaging annuity techniques qualify where it says "by any other means", its should say, "for greater certainty this means income averaging-annuity contracts."
Since we cannot now have IAAC under the present budget, let us have it under the Farm Credit Corporation. Let us say that of the millions of dollars invested in the Farm Credit Corporation, when some farmer sells off his cattle and wants to spread his income over five years or ten years, he can invest his money in the Farm Credit Corporation at half interest rates and pay his tax each year as he gets his income. Let the Farm Credit Corporation do its duty, get access to all the money it needs, through a principle under which no one suffers, and everyone benefits. Thus we will help the minister by putting this so-called redundant amendment of mine in the legislation. I do not think it will be ruled out of order, Mr. Speaker, on the basis of precedent. It can only be ruled out of order under the "con" arguments of a lawyer who tries to say it is already cleared up, when we know from the history of the last 20 years that it is not clear.
We have a committee called the Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. It hears hundreds of cases like those I have enunciated here. It tries to put them on the Order Paper to get something done about them; but for every one mistake it finds, there are hundreds that never get action. Let us not add to the mistakes of this Parliament-and they are many-in this particular case. The minister does have a good bill, he does have a good organization here in the Farm Credit Corporation, but he lacks the money to do what he wants to do, with an interest rate under
which it would be possible to make farming pay. I am sure the government will back him. All we are doing is putting a little crimp into those smart guys who draft the regulations and attempt to tell us that this was not necessarily directed by Parliament. That word "may" does not force them to do anything. Therefore, I am asking for co-operation from all members of the House in having this amendment accepted. The amendment is not expressing the view of just one political party or another, it is really speaking on behalf of all members, members who may some day be ministers and have the job of administering laws that Parliament has passed, only to be scuttled by an abuse which comes from the misuse of the word "may", and the particular language which we have to follow in the legislation. I hope other amendments of the same nature will come forward. I hope this amendment will be accepted.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan ([Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: FARM CREDIT ACT FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, later on I will touch on the presentation made by the hon. member concerning this bill. As Minister of Agriculture I must admit that I agree with much of what he says. I also have the legal advisers which he talked about, and ministers who are not lawyers, but have to make decisions, still have to depend on them to some extent. I will touch on that point later.
It gives me great pleasure to address the House on this most important topic, the amendment to the Farm Credit Act. We have had occasion in the House and in the standing committee to thoroughly discuss and present our views as Members of Parliament on this subject. It gives me great satisfaction to note the general unanimity of support given to this bill and to the work of the Farm Credit Corporation, which is apparent if one reads the speeches in the House or the minutes of the committee. The interest and support expressed by Members of Parliament is a direct reflection of that expressed in the farming community. Credit has become the most critical issue to the survival of many producers today. Therefore, I see it as vital to agriculture that the Farm Credit Corporation be allowed to expand its access to funds.
Many related topics were put forward by members during our deliberations. These concerns cannot all be reflected in this piece of legislation, but I wish to assure members that I have taken note of them. Bill C-88 is an integral part of the total approach the government will be developing as part of the agri-food strategy.
I would now like to take a few moments to recapitulate the main points being proposed in Bill C-88. Clause 8 provides the Farm Credit Corporation with the authority to borrow from sources other than the Consolidated Revenue Fund. The hon. member who just spoke made reference to this step as being a giant step forward. The Farm Credit Corporation is currently funded entirely by loans from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. This amendment would allow FCC to complement these borrowings with funds from the financial markets. In addition to bonds or debentures, special investment instruments could be offered which could be especially attractive to farmers,
March 29, 1982

particularly retiring farmers who wish to retain their investments in agriculture.
Total long-term credit extended to farmers from all sources in Canada has risen by over 20 per cent annually from an estimated $655 million in 1975 to an estimated $1.9 billion in 1980. Until recently, the FCC supplied over 70 per cent of all long-term farm credit extended. In 1980, the Farm Credit Corporation extended 26 per cent of the total long-term credit and was expected to extend about 20 per cent in 1981. Budgetary restraints, rapidly increasing capital values and changing economic conditions haved placed additional pressures on the Farm Credit Corporation to meet the growing demand for long-term credit. The amendment to allow the corporation to borrow from the financial markets will help the corporation to meet this demand for increased funds. Through time, as the mechanisms for borrowing are put in place and the corporation establishes itself in the financial markets, a progressively larger proportion of its funds could be obtained directly from the financial markets.
Clause 7 would increase the capital of the Farm Credit Corporation from $150 million to $225 million. The corporation's borrowing authority is limited to 25 times the capital- that is in Section 13 of the act. The maximum borrowing authority will be reached early in 1982-83. This amendment would thus increase the corporation's borrowing authority from $3.75 billion to $5,625 billion.
Clause 2(2) relates to the expansion of the definition of farming to include any other husbandry activity prescribed by the corporation. As currently defined in the act, farming includes livestock raising, beekeeping, dairying, fruit growing and all tillage of the soil. In addition to the activities currently defined as farming, this amendment would authorize the corporation to prescribe in writing any other husbandry activity as farming for the purposes of the act.
The present definition is inclusive and creates some ambiguity. With agricultural practices changing and new and varied enterprises being introduced, the amendment would allow the corporation to designate husbandry activities as "farming," as required. Since these entreprises are often high risk, it is often difficult for farmers to obtain appropriate private sector financing. With the flexibility provided by the proposed definition, the Farm Credit Corporation can more adequately address the needs of those venturing into new and changing production practices.
Clauses 19 and 20 remove the present 35-year age limitation for loans to phase in farmers and remove the requirement for life insurance in the case of certain of these loans. The Farm Credit Act presently gives the FCC the authority to make loans to applicants under 35 years of age when farming is not their principal occupation, but intend to make farming their principal occupation within five years of receiving the loan. This restriction is considered to be incompatible with the spirit of the Canadian Human Rights Act. Removal of the restriction would allow applicants of any age to participate in the phase-in program.
Farm Loans
Clause 11 provides the authority for the corporation to disperse up to 30 per cent of a loan on the basis of acceptable security until such time as the mortgage registration and other security requisites for the loan are completed. At present, the Farm Credit Corporation makes loans on the security of mortgages on farm lands or farm lands and chattels. Currently, no mortgage advance is made unless the mortgage registration is completed in accordance with provincial requirements. This amendment would help to meet the needs of more farmers since the corporation would be able to disperse up to 30 per cent of the loan before the long process of mortgage documentation is completed.
Again, as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) said, many times it is lawyers who are putting it on the back burner and not really handling it as fast and efficiently as we would like to see. But there are circumstances which sometimes do not allow them to move as fast as they could.
The dispersement of a portion of a loan prior to mortgage registration would save farmers the cost and inconvenience of interim financing until the mortgage funds from the corporation are available. For example, this would assist farmers who must make a payment to initiate a land transaction or to make a cash payment to a building supplier to take advantage of a discount. There are other ways in which this could be an advantage, but I will not touch on them now.
Clause 9 provides that the corporation, with the approval of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), may maintain accounts in its own name in any bank or financial institution in or out of Canada. The corporation presently is limited to maintaining accounts in its own name in the Bank of Canada or in chartered banks designated by the Minister of Finance. This amendment would provide more banking flexibility which would improve the cash management opportunities of the corporation and its financial performance.
For example, should the Farm Credit Corporation at some time be able to borrow Canadian dollars at a lower rate of interest in the Eurobond market than in the Canadian financial markets, this banking flexibility would allow the FCC to make the necessary banking arrangements to accommodate the administration of such transactions.
A further amendment set forth in this bill provides that the maximum amount of a loan which may be oustanding to an applicant or applicants be prescribed by regulation rather than in the act. Currently, the limits specified in the act are $200,000 when there is one qualifying applicant in a farming enterprise, and $400,000 when there is more than one. It is no secret that financing of farming operations is getting more and more expensive all the time. Many people do not realize this. If the Farm Credit Corporation is to meet the needs of modern agriculture, it must have the flexibility to adjust the loan maximum upwards when necessary. Transferring the loan limits from the act to regulation will provide an opportunity for the corporation to respond more quickly to changing

March 29, 1982
Farm Loans
agricultural conditions. At this time we are proposing to increase these limits to $300,000 for one qualifying applicant, and $500,000 when there is more than one applicant.
Part II of the bill represents the authority needed by the Farm Credit Corporation to rebate five percentage points on loans made under the special farm financial assistance program. This authority will allow me to obtain the funds through the departmental estimates.
I would like to take this opportunity to report on this program which ends on Wednesday of this week, March 31. As of March 15 the Farm Credit Corporation had approved $44.7 million of the $45.4 million allocation to the program. That does not sound like a magnificent sum, but it represents tremendous importance to 368 borrowers.
The breakdown by region is as follows: British Columbia, 15 loans, $3,347,200; Alberta, 20 loans, $4 million; Saskatchewan, 48 loans, $5,610,290; Manitoba, 42 loans, $5,998,800; Ontario, 123 loans, $15,362,500; Quebec, 82 loans,$6,954,800; the Atlantic provinces, 38 loans, $3,240,700. The total is $44,514,290. We know that the balance of the program will be used up or has been spoken for already. This progrm reflects only a part of a special effort of the government to provide assistance to farmers in serious financial difficulty.
The small business bond has been extended to a great number of farmers who would not have had access to these lower interest rate loans from the banks prior to the budget announcement. In a number of cases the farmers' problems were solved by a combination of the two programs. We were successful in many instances where the Farm Credit Corporation, the farmer and the local bank manager worked out a very good program. Where the Farm Credit Corporation lent the maximum to the individual, the small business bond would be used by the banker in many cases. This happened in not nearly as many cases as we would have liked, but it did in many cases. I have only touched on the highlights of the bill to re-emphasize the impact of this legislation.
In response to the hon. member's motion to amend Section 13(1), I would like to point out-the hon. member will dispute this, as some other hon. members will-that this section presently allows the FCC to borrow by any means and does not exclude the concept of Small Business Development Bond. However, after listening to the hon. member, I can understand that his amendment is somewhat different from just Small Business Development Bond. As I understand this amendment, the hon. member would like to see the FCC borrow funds by issuing bonds-not necessarily small business bonds-to investors. Because the return to the investors would be given special tax consideration, the cost of funds to the FCC would be reduced. The benefit of the lower costs of funds could then be transferred to farmers who would borrow from the Farm Credit Corporation. My advisers say this would require amendments to the current-

I want to say something again about what the hon. member has proposed. He has dealt further tonight with what he wants to do with this. I do not think he and I disagree very much. My advisers tell me that I have the authority to move into the bond market and so forth, but moving in such a way would mean granting the corporation more authority than has ever before been granted any corporation. We want to make sure we are doing this right.
I had a meeting with the minister of agriculture of the province of Ontario today, and one of the things he is concerned about is where I am at, where the government is at or where Parliament is at with respect to the Farm Credit Corporation bill. The province of Ontario has a program to provide for immediate cash flow, but the provincial government sees a need for the national lending institution to move long-term credit. We had discussions about long-term credit, how much is being used in Canada today and who is making it possible. I think he agreed-although he might not have put it in such language as to say he was agreeing with me 100 per cent-that the private lending institutions have not understood rural Canada when it comes to long-term credit. A good many farmers in difficulty are farmers who, if they had been given
March 29, 1982

really long-term credit at reasonable rates of interest, would not be in the difficulty they are in today.
Again I come back to the Farm Credit Corporation. That corporation probably has more ability, knowledge and experience in understanding agriculture and rural Canada than any other lending institution, because that has been its job since it was conceived and put together. We want more money. We want the corporation to move back into lending. We would like it to be lending not just 20 per cent of long-term money but perhaps 60 per cent in the next year or at least the next two years.
We would like the corporation to recoup its position as the main lender. We would like the corporation to lend not just to those in dire straits, and not just to be the lender of last resort, but to lend to farmers-I believe the hon. member said this- for any need in rural Canada. If we can raise this kind of money, then I am sure what the hon. member opposite has said and what I have said about the future of agriculture and the challenge that exists in agriculture is true. It is going to need the kind of lending program, the kind of institution that understands the situation so it can forge ahead and provide the kind of financial lending program necessary for farmers.
In Canada today there are 320,000 farmers and it is forecast that within the next 18 years 425,000 farmers will be needed to produce the food that is necessary, not only to look after our expanding population but also to take care of the needs of millions of people in other parts of the world. Canada is one of the few countries which can undertake to do that. We have the ability, the land, the technology and the scientific information that is necessary.
Many countries, big and small, developed and developing, are envious of our agricultural production. They are amazed at what we do in this land of ice and snow. They might be more amazed, Mr. Speaker, at what we could do if we pass this bill speedily. If we could do that, then we could provide the things that are necessary for agriculture, and by helping agriculture, help all of society.

A cooperative insurance company is taxed in the same way as any other insurance company. It does not benefit from special taxing privileges as some people believe. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening to speak to the amendment to the Farm Credit Corporation Act offered by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) in which he attempts to clarify the language contained in the act. I think the minister has given the reaction of the legal profession to that amendment. I am not going to spend too much time arguing for or against the need for clarity in the language of the act. Generally speaking, I think bills such as the one before
15932

March 29, 1982
Farm Loans
us should provide a fair amount of flexibility to the lending institution so it can meet the borrowing needs of farmers. Those needs change very drastically from time to time and I will come to that point later in my remarks.
I should like to comment on some of the argument which occurred in the past few minutes between the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) regarding the reaction of some of the financial institutions to the concept of the small business bond or the agribond or whatever name is attached to the credit instrument that is being proposed. 1 am aware that some of the credit unions are concerned about the use of the bond for the Farm Credit Corporation.
Most hon. members who are present this evening know that to a great extent credit unions get their financing from deposits by people in rural communities. A great many of the deposits in prairie Canada-and I am informed that this is so in Quebec and the maritimes-come from retired farmers. Because they are part of the community and because they believe in the credit union movement and the development of their community through co-operation, they put the proceeds of the sale of their farms back into the credit union. In many instances the credit union lends the funds to the next generation of farmers. This is what most of us have in mind for the agribond or the small business bond concept as it would apply to the Farm Credit Corporation. I think most of us see the financing of agriculture ideally as coming from the retiring generation of farmers who, to a large extent, help finance the new generation of farmers.
We think the problem is not whether the Farm Credit Corporation will receive the deposits that credit unions cannot receive. The problem should be more properly addressed at the level of the Income Tax Act. When this becomes possible, it will be of very little difference to farmers, who are investing or retiring, in which institution they decide to invest moneys from the sale of their businesses. We think that the Income Tax Act should be changed in such a way that it would benefit farmers, whether they use the Farm Credit Corporation or local credit unions. It would strictly become a choice as to which lending institutions they choose to invest money in. There would be no violent shifts in the lending patterns of rural Canadians. The coming generation would have an enlarged pool of capital from which to borrow money to set up business.
All of us in the House recognize the importance of increased amounts of money being made available to farmers, particularly beginning farmers or those who want to expand fairly small operations. We should spend a few moments this evening looking at the real problem in agriculture which developed over the last eight to ten years. I do not think it is strictly one of farmers being short of finances or borrowing power. Rather than strictly a shortage of funds, we in fact have a farm income crisis which is worsening at an ever-increasing rate. If legislators do not start to address the real problem, no amount of increase in funds to the Farm Credit Corporation or to any
other lending institution will cure the problem. The disease is becoming rampant. Net farm incomes across the country have remained relatively the same since 1974. I do not think any other segment of our economy would have to admit to that, but realized net income in the case of Canadian agriculture in 1974 amounted to $3.5 billion. In 1980 it was $9.3 billion. In 1981 it rose to $4 billion, but in 1982 it is expected to drop to $3.4 billion, which is slightly lower than it was in 1974.
In intervening years incomes did not slide very much. In this era farm prices have not risen as fast as their costs. This is not new to agriculture, but it is catching up. Admittedly in that period of time there was rapid inflation in the value of farm assets. In 1974 there was approximately $40 billion in capital tied up in the Canadian agricultural industry. In 1980, according to the figures provided by the Department of Agriculture, those assets approached $100 billion. We see that the value of capital has increased about three times.
From a banking point of view agriculture has been a good bet. The value of assets continues to grow rapidly. Although the amount of money lent by banks and lending institutions has increased rapidly, they feel fairly secure because the market value of the collateral provided by farmers has risen faster. In 1974 there was almost $7 billion of farm debt. In 1980, the last year for which figures are available, it jumped to $16 billion. Approximately $1.8 billion to $2 billion per year of extra debt is accruing to the farm community because incomes do not cover all costs. This is not a healthy situation.
There are other ways to look at investment in agriculture. Turning to 1974 once again, and looking at returns on equity, the amount of income from the collective investment of farmers in agriculture was 10.9 per cent. We must understand what the return on equity figure covers. It does not cover any labour provided by farmers or their families. It does not provide any return for their management capabilities. It is simply a total return which they probably saw as return for labour and management. It is not the method of bookkeeping an average corporation would use, but it gives an idea of what has happened in the last eight years.
In 1974 the return on investment hovered around 10 per cent. In 1980 the return on investment, not counting labour or management abilities, was something under 4 per cent. The estimate for 1982 is not the return on investment Canadian Pacific expects. Unfortunately there are no economists in the Department of Agriculture to perform an analysis of the cost of agricultural production. I hope the government considers hiring a railway economist by the name of Snavely who did a very competent job for the CPR on behalf of the Department of Transport. He assumed that the return on equity before taxes should be 35 per cent and that on money borrowed by the railways it should be 25 per cent. Farmers would be pleased to have such an analysis of their business.
We have done some preliminary work which indicates that wheat farmers, for instance, would receive a return of about $13 per bushel instead of the current $4.30. It would make
March 29, 1982

quite a difference if the same rules were applied to the agricultural community as the government is willing to apply to large corporations such as the railways.
Farm debts are increasing at a rapid rate. Payments for interest have risen from $473 million in 1974 to $1.6 billion in 1980 and by the end of 1981 it was estimated that they would be well in excess of $2 billion. The rate of increase in the cost of interest was approaching six times and the value of farm capital rose about three times. Realized net incomes remained the same, although 1982 dollars purchase less than half that of 1974 dollars. I hope we are beginning to understand just why many farmers are facing bankruptcy and why farmers are wanting to sell out, looking for buyers but often finding there is no one interested. This situation occurred because of a real decline in net incomes, together with the extra debt farmers had to accumulate at a time when interest rates more than doubled. 1 think that explains why the cost of maintaining the credit end of farming has increased more than six times since 1974.
What can we do about this? I think Bill C-88 is an attempt to get some money to help farmers who need to borrow even more in order to stay in business a few additional years. But that is only a temporary solution. A real solution has to be more long term. But if there are long-term solutions found, it does not mean we in the House of Commons and others across the country can sit down and do nothing.
Canada's agricultural producers require a decent level of stabilization immediately so they can begin to recover at least their cost of production. To prevent that from being too expensive for federal and provincial treasuries most farm commodities need a better marketing system. They need the kind of marketing system that will extract the maximum from the free market. Some commodities are covered under marketing boards which come close to doing that, but they cannot always extract the full cost of production from the market. Occasionally they will need assistance from the public purse by way of stabilization programs. Those two things go together so the public purse does not get ripped off. There has to be marketing organizations to do the best job possible in the free market.
Our party has been saying for years that we need adequate marketing boards for the various farm commodities, and as an adjunct there must be stabilization programs to see that farm incomes are adequate to continue to refinance agriculture from year to year. Various farm organizations have been telling us this same thing. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture presented a brief to us during our hearings. We heard similar statements for the National Farmers Union. Recently all Members of Parliament had calls from a group called the Canadian Farmers' Survival Association. That association told us there was a need for an immediate moratorium on receiverships and liquidations. They told us it was time to reinstate the old Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, to bring it up to date, put into effect from 1981 so that farmers would not be
Farm Loans
forced out of their homes and off their land. They told us it was time to reinstate some of the programs established in the 1930s under the ARDA program whereby the government could buy the farm from the farmer and allow him to lease it back, giving the farmer a home and a source of income for up to ten years, after which he could arrange to repurchase the farm.
To some extent this is reminiscent of the land bank program in the province of Saskatchewan which was introduced during hard times in 1971. Farmers having difficulty remaining in the business were given an opportunity to refinance by selling their land to the land bank, using the proceeds to pay off their debts, to increase their capitalization in buildings and equipment and to get on a sound financial base. They had full tenure on that land until the age of 65 or until such time as they wanted to buy it back, which could occur after a five-year period. Some parts of the country have initiated similar programs. It is time the federal government and federal institutions started to look at these approaches in order to solve what I consider to be the real problem.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about the amendment proposed by one of the members on the other side. If I understand correctly, the purpose of the amendment is to have the corporation borrow money by issuing bonds of a type that are currently known as small business development bonds. Since in this case, the investor's income is subject to a special tax rate, it would reduce the corporation's financing costs. This reduction in costs could then be passed on to farmers borrowing from the Farm Credit Corporation. Mr. Speaker, it is true that in present day agriculture, financing is extremely important, since family farms have expanded to the point that hundreds of thousands of dollars are invested in these enterprises. It is obvious that if we are to have viable farms, they must be mechanized and modernized. Especially today, the challenge to the Canadian farmer is increasing, because with the policies introduced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in recent years, there is increasing pressure on Canadian farmers to produce more food for developing countries.
Setting up all these mechanisms will cost money, and Canadian agriculture and Canadian farmers cannot afford to

March 29, 1982
Farm Loans
turn their backs on these developments if they want to maintain their outstanding record. To make agriculture a paying proposition, we shall also have to use our marketing boards and make an extra effort to give farm producers a reasonable level of income security. Our agriculture may be the best in the world and our productivity as well, but if we cannot provide farmers with the assurance of a steady income from agriculture, I feel that even if we give our farmers the best tools on the market, they will not be able to cope with the problems that may occur in this area, considering the seasonality of many crops. In fact, marketing boards and productivity and the rest is not enough. We need other tools such as, for instance, Canagrex, for which legislation has passed first reading, and we hope that this bill will prove to be a very useful mechanism for our farm producers. Since Canagrex, which is so fittingly seen as a corporation responsible for exporting Canadian farm products to world markets, will emerge as a go-between through which all levels of government will be able to enter into government-to-government dealings, many competing forces which might have been unpleasant from the beginning will be eliminated and will no longer exert pressures on the backs of the farm producers.
Still we have had some good news concerning Canadian pork producers since a very dangerous infectious disease has just struck the hog population in Denmark, and this has brought about an increase of about 10 cents a pound in the price of Canadian pork in the last few days, and it is forecast that Canadian pork prices will continue to increase on the Canadian market by perhaps 10 cents more. Such a disaster is unfortunate for hog producers in Denmark, but in view of the seriousness of this disease, we have been informed that Danish hogs may be quarantined for six months to five years depending on the extent of the disease. Of course, everyone will agree that the Japanese market, which was supplied mostly by the Danish producers, will have to turn to the Canadian market. The United States also was importing much of its pork from Denmark and will now have to turn to the Canadian producers. All I want to say, Mr. Speaker, is that after a disastrous period for Canadian hog producers, this will probably have good results for them.
As for our western beef producers, they have entered a cyclical production period and they are now facing many marketing problems. Of course, for some time now, they may have failed to develop the tools which we believe they should have, but as anyone will agree, it is not up to the Canadian government to tell Canadian farm producers which tools they should use to be more prosperous or improve their profitability. Of course, as he wanted himself, the Minister of Agriculture has wished sincerely-and I believe that this is also the wish of the Canadian government-that the Canadian beef industry would submit a program which would provide for better marketing and better research and perhaps enable them to offer their products under other forms which could increase Canadian consumption.
Once again, all this is related to marketing and it would perhaps be useful for our Canadian producers to promote the
nutritional value of Canadian beef, which I believe to be among the best in the world. Mr. Speaker, we have spoken in the past about the productivity of our Canadian producers. This is, of course, a matter of comparison in the North American context. The United States, which produces all year round, have not succeeded in getting that much ahead of us. That is to say that if we compare the total production cost for farmers in the United States and in Canada, even with a climate which allows the Americans to produce twelve months a year, the difference in the cost of farm production is no more than 1 per cent. You must therefore agree, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian producers are at the forefront of progress and are constantly improving. And I will also make a comparison that may hint at a possible solution-we saw that Canadian milk producers during 1974 and 1975 had to cope with tremendous problems, survival problems because they were selling below cost.
It will be remembered that in 1976, on Parliament Hill, right here in Ottawa, thousands of Canadian milk producers demonstrated against the fact that the Canadian government had imposed a quota system. Possibly this was one of the first major products for which the government imposed some form of a quota system because all across Canada dairy farmers were producing without being aware of the needs of our domestic market, and in so doing helped create tremendous surpluses that were costing millions of dollars in storage costs. Therefore, the imposition of quotas may have been a somewhat difficult decision to make in 1976, but Quebec producers now enjoy what may be the best dairy policy in the world. So much so that recently the Americans came to Ottawa to look at that policy and see what benefits it could have in the United States.
The fact is that in the United States today it costs $250,000 an hour for storing surplus dairy products, and this amounts to approximatly $2 billion a year in storage charges and American surpluses are getting larger and larger. And this year we are told also that there will be further increases in the number of milch cows in the United States. Therefore, the freewheeling type of marketing they have in the United States only tends to weaken the American industry. Again, the Canadian government must be commended for having had that courage, and as I said, it must be acknowledged that in 1976 fixing a quota on Canadian production was a difficult decision to make. Producers always had been in the habit of producing at whatever cost, so creating surpluses. Therefore, we might take a hint from that in our future farm policies, the marketing board approach that was then imposed but today is giving farmers an ever-increasing sense of security. Let us hope, Mr. Speaker, that the policy currently under negotiation will maintain that policy over the coming fiscal year to the benefit of our Canadian milk producers.
I would like to comment further on this amendment, because the proposal certainly deserves consideration and, of course, it is now under study. However, since clause 13 does not exclude the small business bonds, the amendment put forward by my hon. colleague may not be required, because somehow the Income Tax Act should be amended accordingly.
March 29, 1982

Currently, the Canadian Farm Credit Corporation seems to be more and more generous and I hope Canadians will use it in the best possible way because, as I said, Canadian farm financing is getting more and more complex by reason of our needs and of our high production levels. If we are to maintain that high productivity rate producers will obviously need additional financing. But, as we have seen so well in the bill before the House, and in the history of the Farm Credit Corporation, Canadian farm producers have at their disposal considerable sources of financing which take into account production costs, the cost of farm equipment and the cost of land.
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, should we, together, feel that there is need for other sources of financing, then so much the better for the Canadian farmer, provided that money is well spent and also that the cost of borrowing it does not price our products out of the market, since other countries may offer those same products at lower prices. But I have confidence in our Canadian farmers who have always managed to produce at competitive prices in the past. So, it is to be hoped that every stage of this bill, which will be of benefit to all Canadian farmers, especially in these difficult times when they are increasingly in need of financing, will be passed by the House.

I would like to deal more specifically with the report stage of Bill C-88. We basically support this legislation because it would allow the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow supplemental funds from the private marketplace, it would increase the board of directors from five to seven members, it would remove the 35-year-old age limitation on Section 33 loans, and it would update some of the language used in the Farm Credit Corporation legislation. I earlier shared with the House the fact that we basically support this legislation, as do the majority of farm groups throughout Canada. I want to state that we on this side are very disappointed that this minister of agriculture has not given agriculture the priority it merits. In reality, the farmers of Canada have been neglected for the past ten years.
I was first elected in 1974 and I remember the election campaign. The farming population had a great deal of respect for our Minister of Agriculture, but that respect has turned sour and cynical simply because he has not lived up to the repeated commitment he has given to the farming population throughout Canada. The record will show that farm bankruptcies have increased by some 50 per cent this past year. The November 12 budget introduced by his government has been a disaster to the farming population in Canada. The many budget provisions, as they pertain to income-averaging annuities and capital gains provisions, are disastrous. This Minister of Agriculture promised he would do something about the capital gains provisions. Instead, they have worsened as they relate to the farming sector. In relation to the capital cost allowances which the farming population has traditionally enjoyed, this budget will increase the tax payable in the first year in which farm machinery is purchased.

He finally indicated that he would allow the province to participate. The province of Alberta itself has had to introduce programs relating to the beef and sheep industries. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to note that as usual at this time, the gallery is filled with newspapermen who have come to hear us and to report the facts as I will put them before my colleagues this evening. During the past seven or eight weeks, that is almost two months, the Quebec Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Jean Garon has taken pleasure in publicly making a series of serious but false accusations concerning New Brunswick seed potatoes.
Seed potatoes are used to eventually produce potatoes for human consumption, but it does not mean that seed potatoes are not fit for human consumption. On the contrary, they are top quality potatoes. However, the Quebec Minister of Agriculture is accusing, on the one hand, the federal Department of Agriculture and, on the other hand, the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island producers, of having sold and shipped contaminated seed potatoes to Quebec producers. Now, it often happens that Mr. Garon is mistaken, but this time he is utterly mistaken because he is talking through his hat.
We know that, historically, the potato production in the province of Quebec has been low compared with that of both New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, which alone produced for years almost 50 per cent of the total Canadian production. With time, of course, this rate of production has not decreased in terms of volume or total cultivated lands, but some western provinces as well as Ontario have become more competitive at the production level. But what is most serious about the accusation made my Mr. Garon is that he offhandedly condemns all seed potato stock originating from New Brunswick, without producing any irrefutable and sound supporting evidence. On the contrary, the Department of Agriculture and its food and vegetable certification division

March 29, 1982
Adjournment Debate
have an outstanding record throughout the world. This reputation has been acquired after decades of great sacrifices and hard work and Mr. Garon, the Quebec agriculture minister, would offhandedly ruin this outstanding reputation. Well, Mr. Garon, as I have just mentioned, has not been able to produce any sound evidence. On the contrary, the Department of Agriculture of the Government of Canada had to remind him that on several occasions it had to ask the Quebec government to implement a consumer potato production control program within its own territory because the seed potato stock were grown on the same lands on which uncontrolled consumer potato stock had been grown the preceding year.
On the other hand, in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, producers have been trying for many years to eradicate a number of diseases of which the most serious by far is the bacterial ring rot, which is perhaps the most tenacious and unpredictable, because it is very difficult to identify. As some Quebec producers had bought potatoes in New Brunswick and sold them again to Quebec growers whose crops where affected by bacterial ring rot, Mr. Garon automatically inferred that the origin of the disease is in New Brunswick. Which is simply not true, because inspectors of the federal Department of Agriculture returned to visit the operation of the New Brunswick producer, check a number of stocks which had been produced on his farm and distributed not only in Quebec, but throughout the Atlantic region, but failed to find any evidence of bacterial ring rot.
Therefore it appears that, according to this very strict control, the origin of the bacterial ring rot is unfortunate, and I say it is unfortunate because the bacterial ring rot is a very serious disease which exists quite often in a latent state practically everywhere in the world if people are not careful. This disease could very well be traced to the soil itself in Quebec, to warehouses in Quebec, to bags, trucks, tractors, who knows where it could be traced to, but it is a fact that it can be traced to any of those places. Given the lack of control in Quebec over the seed potato, Mr. Garon cannot state categorically that the disease could not already be found in the soil in Quebec, that it could not be found on certain farms which supplied the producers of the regions of Temiscouata, Riviere-du-Loup and Kamouraska, which border on New Brunswick. By making such sweeping accusations, Mr. Garon therefore hinders the entire potato industry in Canada and tarnishes our good reputation in foreign countries. I suggest that the federal government agriculture minister was right to ask Mr. Garon to refrain from making that type of public statements.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Dionne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) stated last week when answering a question
about the bacterial ring rot, I must confess that the Quebec agriculture minister, Mr. Garon, created quite a deplorable situation. Mr. Garon's allegations caused great harm both to the reputation of New Brunswick potato producers and to the federal inspection service.
Following the allegations that Mr. Garon chose to make to the press instead of contacting him to try and find a solution to the problem, the Minister of Agriculture said that he would not be drawn into Mr. Garon's political games. He also indicated to his Quebec colleague that if he was really interested in solving this problem, he would certainly find the time to discuss it with him. The agriculture minister and Mr. Garon met last Monday, but unfortunately, they could not come to an agreement. However, Mr. Garon presented a file with compensation claims totalling more than $1 million from the Quebec potato producers affected by the bacterial ring rot. Agriculture Canada officials are now studying this file and the agriculture minister promised Mr. Garon an answer in a few days.
As far as the federal government is concerned I can say unequivocally that the Federal Potato Inspection Service is among the best in the world.
I can also guarantee that during the course of the very thorough investigation and chronological study conducted by the department about this contamination, all the facts have been checked. Mr. Garon indicated that the ring rot was caused by a shipment of seed potatoes from New Brunswick. After checking at the source, we have found that the producer has not had any problem with bacterial ring rot for approximately 20 years. We have checked other potatoes grown on the same farm which have been shipped all over Canada, without finding any trace of bacterial ring rot.
As usual, Mr. Garon had the urge to provoke an ideological debate between Agriculture Canada and the Quebec government. In my opinion, this is unfortunate since all Canadian potato producers have suffered serious prejudice as a result of this, and we hope, Mr. Speaker, that this problem will be solved as it should be, that is by experts.

subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-RESTRUCTURING OF FINANCING OF ASSOCIATION CANADIENNE FRANCHISE DE L'ONTARIO
OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-RESTRUCTURING OF FINANCING OF ASSOCIATION CANADIENNE FRANCHISE DE L'ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday, March 23, I directed a question to the Secretary of State (M. Regan) concerning the restructuring of financing of the ACFO announced on February 16 by the parliamentary secretary to the minister. I would like to go over the situation again, because I feel the decision taken by the Secretary of State may be harmful to Franco-Ontarians by depriving them of a provincial organization which has proved to be a much needed protector of their rights. It all started when the Department of the Secretary of State told the media of a new policy concerning the administration of the official languages branch.
March 29, 1982

As a result of that policy, the Secretary of State intends to redirect some of the funds to the regional councils of the ACFO, thus bypassing the provincial organization.
Still according to the Secretary of State, the purpose of those new policies was to thwart the tendency of overstructuring which afflicts organizations active in minority groups, the ACFO included, of course, in an attempt to get closer to the membership.
That is the purpose of those administrative changes. Let us examine the problems created by the Secretary of State's intervention. They are threefold: there is the legal problem, the interference problem and the methods problem. First, the judicial problem. The ACFO is a legal entity from which derive 19 regional councils that have no other status than that granted by the ACFO charter and amendable only with the consent of the general assembly of the organization. Moreover, the ACFO has 17 affiliates. The present proposal creates a problem since, in fact, it alters the ACFO's legal structure without the consent of the general assembly. Indeed in putting forward the dissatisfaction of some regional councils and the desire to decentralize the intent is to make them independent of the provincial organization by financing them directly. As those regional branches do not exist outside ACFO, it will be necessary to establish new structures and corporations, before any money can be provided for them.
This is where the Department of the Secretary of State's interference comes about. Six regional branches of an independent organization, as demonstrated by the consultation held during the first week of March, are dissatisfied with the present situation. They want to get more power, hence their interest in the department's proposal. All the same, 13 regional branches show their support for the provincial ACFO. Without any right to do so, the Department of the Secretary of State supports the six branches, and I can assure you that in the future they will come directly under the department for their funding. There we have interference pure and simple in the internal business of an independent organization. If the regions want more decentralization, it is incumbent on the provincial ACFO to respond to their request. Whether or not it is done in co-operation with the Department of the Secretary of State is not the problem. But the provincial ACFO must be involved as the only organization legally responsible for its regional councils. The Department of the Secretary of State's proposal is rather strange when considered more closely. Because a minority of dissenters refuse to play the game of democracy, and although 13 regional branches out of 19 support the provincial ACFO, the department decides to give the minority of six their own way. It is as if a dissatisfied province wanted to sever all ties with the federal structure and were granted autonomy without consultation with its federal partners.
Adjournment Debate
Should we see in this new approach a step toward a new type of federation? The last problem, Mr. Speaker, is rather a moral one, and it concerns the offhand behaviour of the Secretary of State in this matter. As a matter of fact, allegedly to get nearer to the grass roots, the Secretary of State never held any consultations prior to announcing his decision. Everyone learned of that decision through the press. Furthermore, the present proposal is not supported by any document. I had to write twice to the minister and to phone him before I could meet him, and he announced only last week, in an answer he gave me in this House, that he was going to meet with officials of ACFO late last week. One can only note the department's reticent and unco-operative bureaucratic attitude in this matter. That is why I ask the minister today to table actual documents summing up the present proposal for restructuring ACFO.
It is to be hoped that the spirit of dialogue and co-operation, which was apparent, albeit slightly, at the meeting of March 25 will be conducive to a new protocol of agreement that will satisfy all parties. Although ACFO had every right to resent the actions of the Secretary of State, it nevertheless approached the minister at the March 25 meeting in the hope of finding common ground for an understanding. Through a written proposal, ACFO made a breakthrough on this issue. This proposal which, as I understand will be released in the near future, satisfies the requirements of all parties involved. The decentralization that everybody wishes for should provide the dissenting regions with a solution to their problems. On the other hand, the role of the ACFO would be maintained in that it would remain the provincial association of Franco-Ontari-ans, thus avoiding any legal issue. Furthermore, as decentralization was sought in the first place by the Department of the Secretary of State as well as the power to directly fund regional associations, I believe the minister should support such proposal which meets all his wishes. Mr. Speaker, any compromise involves a certain amount of give and take. But in its proposal the ACFO seems prepared to go all the way, having already made a more generous offer than the other party. I hope the department will react positively to this proposal and will show a similar desire to settle the matter to the satisfaction of all concerned.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean Lapierre (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Sports); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-RESTRUCTURING OF FINANCING OF ASSOCIATION CANADIENNE FRANCHISE DE L'ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the result of remarks made by the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), on March 25, the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) met with the officials of ACFO in the presence of the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier. At that time, ACFO made a proposal and with the cooperation of all concerned, we are now in consultation with the seven regional associations interested in dealing directly with the Department of the Secretary of State. During that meeting, the Secretary of State offered to review his position, perhaps very soon, after consultation with the seven regional associations; and if those associations agreed with the ACFO

March 29, 1982
Adjournment Debate
proposal we would give favourable consideration to that proposal. If the seven decide to use the provincial association as a banker or to stay within the provincial association and to deal directly with it, the Secretary of State has no objection to that either. But our responsibilities toward the taxpayers and those seven entities which have said democratically that they wanted to deal directly with the Secretary of State must be considered. I think that is strictly what is at stake, and the member for Ottawa-Vanier is well aware of the situation. He has complained of having nothing in writing. I think that more than anybody else he had access to inside information and had discussions on the subject with the present Secretary of State.
I am convinced that the inquiries and mediation attempts by the member for Ottawa-Vanier will lead us to the best solution. One thing is sure, the Secretary of State is bound to take his responsibilities toward taxpayers and to be receptive to the needs of minority groups across Canada. This is part of his mandate. The decision that was made was specifically designed to respond to the expectations of some communities across Ontario, and it was made simply to get closer to the grass roots.
My hon. colleague's three objections were strictly legal. I think a lawyer could always find a satisfactory solution, and I really do not know whether it is a major problem. As far as any interference is concerned, he who pays the piper usually calls the tune. We hope that this movement toward decentralization and toward working with communities will not be seen as interference but rather as an attempt to be more in tune with the taxpayers and to spend money where they would like to see it spent.
Finally, as far as the method is concerned, of course one can always consult ad nauseam, but my hon. colleague is probably aware that where difficult decisions of this kind are concerned, consultation takes place a few days beforehand, but in the final instance, the decision is made in consultation with local authorities and departmental officers in whom we have full confidence.
