subtopic: FREEDOM OF INFORMATION-PROPOSAL TO DELAY PASSAGE OF LEGISLATION. (B) CROWN PRIVILEGE AND JUDICIAL REVIEW
FREEDOM OF INFORMATION-PROPOSAL TO DELAY PASSAGE OF LEGISLATION. (B) CROWN PRIVILEGE AND JUDICIAL REVIEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate this evening arises out of a question I asked the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) on February 12. You will recall the Minister of Communications on the subject of freedom of information received a letter from the provincial attorney general of Ontario speaking on his own behalf and on behalf of other attorneys general. In essence, the provincial governments were asking the federal government to stop consideration in the committee or elsewhere of its freedom of information bill in order to deal with a freedom of information bill to be agreed upon by all 11 governments of Canada.
Surely, no one has to tell this House of Commons how unlikely it is we would ever get agreement on a freedom of information bill of that scope.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that we worked 54 years to get agreement on the Constitution. I wager the parliamentary secretary would be greyer than he is today, and both he and I would be drawing the old age pension well before a bill would even see the light of day in draft form. I say to you that, following the tradition of federal-provincial agreements with respect to this matter, any freedom of information bill to result would pale in comparison to Bill C-43, the freedom of information bill which this government advanced. It would be useless. It would be without teeth. It would be blind. It would be full of so many notwithstanding clauses that no one interested in freedom of information could ever countenance that kind of delay. I do not countenance it.
If you scratch a little deeper, Messrs. McMurtry, Romanow and company are interested in much more than that. They do not want independent judicial review. They do not want to do away with Crown privilege. They are afraid of that. They want the governments of Canada-and I put government in the plural-to be the judge, the jury and the policemen with respect to what information will be released.
I do not think I have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that without independent judicial review any freedom of information law would be next to useless, particularly if the decision as to what would be released were left to the people who held the information being asked for. It is as simple as that.
I hope the parliamentary secretary will tell the House tonight that his minister, the Minister of Communications, and his colleagues in the government will not fall for that line of baloney of 11 governments, because that is what it is. If they do, it will be an incredible about face on the part of this government.
In 1979, I introduced a freedom of information bill, imperfect in many respects, the first word, but not the last. In 1980, the present government introduced Bill C-43 which in some respects was not as good as the one of the Clark government, but in many respects was better. I would be astounded if the government should even consider stopping consideration, or choose not to appear before the committee to complete consideration of the bill. If the government does that, it will complete the breaking of another promise.
Both Bill C-15, my bill, and Bill C-43, the Minister of Communication's bill went to committee after one round of speeches. Gallup polls approve of freedom of information. All parties approve also. Yet after two years a freedom of information bill is still a mirage. I find it impossible to accept the opinions of the provincial attorneys general in this matter, and I find it unpalatable and distasteful to believe that a government which promised freedom of information should fall over in that round-heeled fashion, rather than forging ahead with a bill. The fact of the matter is, and I might as well say it here, the provinces do not want to make freedom of information
March 29, 1982

better. As a result of their suggestion, they want freedom of information legislation dead and buried. I think it is high time the government came to the committee and stated its position. Does it favour that, will it allow the bill to go forward, and will it invite the provinces to appear before the committee like any other witness. Will it now make up the time lost to the cause of freedom of information by the fact that the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), while professing a great interest in freedom of information here, piled up page after page of useless questions in committee on a bill which has a provision calling for parliamentary review three years down the road?
I hope the parliamentary secretary will say to us tonight that the bill will go forward, the blandishments of the provincial attorneys general will be ignored, and the government will live up to the commitment it made in the throne speech. If it does not, then the Minister of Communications and his colleagues in government, from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) down, stand on the same footing as the provincial attorneys general who have shown themselves to be dinosaurs on the subject of freedom of information. I look forward to hearing from the parliamentary secretary.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Masters (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: FREEDOM OF INFORMATION-PROPOSAL TO DELAY PASSAGE OF LEGISLATION. (B) CROWN PRIVILEGE AND JUDICIAL REVIEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say I am grateful for the opportunity provided by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) to discuss the subject of access to information. 1 think all of us know of his deep and abiding interest in and effectiveness on this subject.
As the House is aware, Bill C-43, which contains legislative proposals for both access to information and privacy, was introduced in the House in July, 1980 and received second reading in January, 1981. The Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs undertook its review of the bill in March of last year. A number of groups and experts came before the
Adjournment Debate
committee to give their views. This process took more than two months of the committee's time. Clause by clause examination got under way only in June. The committee has devoted a great number of sittings to the various clauses of the bill; some 45 provisions had been adopted before Christmas out of the more than 160 clauses in the bill.
During the course of the summer, and last fall, the provinces informed the government of their concerns in regard to Bill C-43.1 refer in particular to the very specific objections raised by the attorney general for Ontario, Mr. McMurtry, in relation to the protection of law enforcement information and other important issues in a letter he sent last June to the minister. In November the minister was advised by the spokesman for the provinces that the Ontario letter had received the endorsement of all provinces. Since then discussions have taken place with the provinces at both the ministerial and official levels.
As indicated to the House by the Minister of Communications, representations from a common front made up of most of the provinces must be taken seriously, indeed. I think hon. members from across the aisle, given their fundamental and philosophical commitment to harmonious federal-provincial relations, will agree that the legitimate concerns of the provinces cannot be summarily dismissed. I say to the hon. member that, despite his feelings and our desire, it is in the interest of all concerned that the federal government and the provinces are given an opportunity to iron out outstanding issues in relation to access to information and privacy.
